**It’s probably not very generous to say that any score of 58 in pro golf should come with an asterisk. But we will anyway.**

Japan’s Yuta Suguira played tremendously well in the third round of the Korn Ferry Tour's Compliance Solutions Championship in Owasso, Okla., making 10 birdies and an eagle to shoot 12-under 58 at The Patriot Golf Club. It was the fourth sub-60 score in KFT history, and a bogey kept Suguira from tying the all-time mark of 57 set by Cristobal del Solar’in the 2024 Astara Golf Championship.

We give Suguira an enthusiastic golf clap instead of a throwing our fists in the air for several reasons. The KFT offers pushover courses at times, including the Patriot, which surrendered a 59 last year to Davis Chatfield while Adrien Dumont de Chassart opened with two 61s en route to a record-breaking total of 33 under. As with last year, it doesn’t help the course’s defense that the golfers are playing preferred lies. The scoring average for the round was a KFT-record 66.57, and there were two 60s, including William Sides lipping out a birdie putt on 18 for 59. Is this really the “test” you want in the first of two KFT Finals events?

For his work, Suguira—the 2025 Japan Tour rookie of the year—moved into a tie for eighth heading into Sunday. The leader at 21 under is Trent Phillips, who shot 61 on Saturday.

**There seems to be little that happens quietly in Michael Block’s life.**

He is, after all, the most polarizing golf club pro on the planet, and he continues to make competitive waves on PGA Tour Champions. Block is once again contending for his first senior title this week in the Jefferson Lehigh Valley Classic, taking the clubhouse lead on Saturday by shooting 63. But he doesn’t need a victory to celebrate a big milestone, and that part has gone under the radar.

As [reported by the Daily Breeze](link_39) in Orange County, Block will officially become a member of the over-50 circuit after Lehigh because he'll have made seven starts this season and has earnings that put him well into the top 72 on tour. Block has three top-10s since turning 50 in June and had earned $326,486. That would have put him at No. 50 in the Charles Schwab Cup standings as a member, and he figures to climb farther up with another strong result in Allentown, Pa. So, Block is in the three-event playoffs that begin Oct. 23 at the Stifel Charity Classic in St. Louis—which happens to be his hometown. Just one more crazy Blockie twist.

“I really didn’t think it was a possibility with such a short season left [after turning 50] that I could make the playoffs,” Block told Southland Golf, “but that was my goal—and now it’s going to happen. It’s unbelievable.”

**With two events remaining on the Korn Ferry Tour schedule, it’s the time of year where careers hang in the balance.**

That’s what makes this out-of-this-world par from Nicolo Galletti so impressive. Playing the Compliance Solutions Championship, the 31-year-old was 60th in points, sitting right on the bubble to advance to next week’s KFT Championship. Mid-way through the second round at The Patriot Golf Club in Oklahoma, he was hovering around the projected cut when he hit his tee ball on the par-5 first hole right into the woods. He played a provisional, which went left into a penalty area. Somehow, though, he managed to find his first ball, punched out to 192 yards and eventually got up and down from 35 feet to save par.

Galletti went on to make the cut, but he still has some work to do over the weekend. At T-47 entering the third round, he is projected to drop to 64th in KFT points. But at least he’s got his fate in his hands.

**The Bank of Utah Championship kept arguably its biggest TV viewer and fan draw for the weekend, and Jackson Koivun made even that dramatic.**

Needing to rally to make the cut at the Black Desert Resort, the 21-year-old rookie birdied the 14th and 16th holes but still had to make at least a 4 on the 600-yard, par-5 finisher. And it didn’t look good when Koivun’s tee shot found a fairway bunker. “Didn't have the greatest lie," he recounted. "But I pulled 3-wood and I was, like, ‘I'm going to go for broke here.’ Came out nicely.”

Boy, did it. Koivun hammered that wood from the sand 260 yards and ended up just 43 yards from the flag. From there, clipped a low chip to five feet and made the birdie putt to shoot four-under 67 and finish on the cut number at six under. It's worth watching:

After earning 2½ points in Team USA's win last week, including a singles victory over Si Woo Kim, Koivun admitted on Friday to being “mentally exhausted” and “struggling with some emotions.” And for those reasons, he said, “I’m really proud of the way I fought back on those last nine holes.”

[](link_51)

[Tod Leonard](link_36)

Oct 2

**Kevin Streelman has only two top-10 finishes in the past three years on the PGA Tour and the last of his two career victories came more than a decade ago—in 2014.**

So he was to be forgiven on Friday when he couldn’t remember the last time he’d played in the final group on a weekend. The subject came up because Streelman got into the final three-ball on Saturday for the third round of the Bank of Utah Championship. Guys have been shooting lights out amid the red rocks and black lava fields, and the 47-year-old Streelman went 63-64 to be two shots behind leader Austin Smotherman. Streelman wasn’t originally in the field but got in on his number when Lanto Griffin pulled out. “Very thankful and fortunate to be here. Also, I feel like I have nothing to lose, really,” Streelman said.

Streelman is the definition of a journeyman, having played 19 consecutive seasons on the tour, with 11 more appearances left to reach 500. He could only make 10 starts in 2025 after tearing the meniscus in his knee. “My family's coming in this weekend. I just feel I'm going to try and attack and have fun,” said Streelman, who is 151st in the FedEx Cup and could make a huge jump toward the top 100 with a strong finish.

# My solution for ranking pro golfers might be crazy enough to work

The ongoing World Golf Ranking debate means we need another method for comparing golfers. This is it

By[Sam Weinman](link_33)

 January 12, 2023 

Save for later

For most golfers, the currency that measures our skill is a handicap. It is a measure not only of our scores, but the difficulty of where we play. Both factors are essential.

Why don’t pros need handicaps? Because pros always play straight up, and the handicap’s main purpose is to help players of different abilities arrive at a form of fair competition. But a handicap system among pros—or at least a slight variation—might come in handy somewhere else.

For those not paying attention, professional golf is at an inflection point. [There are competing professional golf tours](link_34), and a series of major championships caught in the middle asked to determine who is eligible to play in them and who isn’t. For now, those majors rely on the Official World Golf Ranking (OWGR) to make many of those calculations, but [that system has critics, too.](link_35)

The central conflict: The OWGR is not granting ranking points for LIV Golf events, which means [LIV players are dropping in the rankings](link_36) and risk being shut out of future majors. Are those players actually getting worse? Not really, and therein lies the problem. Any system dependent on comparing golfers’ performances in specific events becomes problematic the moment you start debating the validity of one tour’s events versus another’s.

But what if the system that assessed players’ merit relied less on _who they played against_ and more on _how they played on specific courses?_ In other words, **what if professional golf had something like its own handicap?**

## Introducing the Pro Golf Handicap

Now, before we go any further with this idea, a couple of caveats. The concept I am floating would at some point rely on a fairly intricate algorithm, but that algorithm should be devised by just about anyone other than this college English major. Second, the reason the current system is flawed is because it contains some inherent bias, and my concept aspires to circumvent the most problematic areas. But some subjectivity is inevitable, so the challenge is to at least place the judgment calls into the least fraught elements.

This will make sense. Stay with me.

Anyway, back to the handicap system, which at its core asks two questions: What did you shoot? And where did you play? You need both because golfers recognize a 70 from the tips at Winged Foot is way more difficult than a 70 on a 5,700-yard course with flat greens and no hazards.

## More From Golf Digest

[![Image 2](https://golfdigest.sports.sndimg.com/content/dam/images/golfdigest/fullset/2023/2/golf-ball-in-hole-centered.jpg.rend.hgtvcom.406.271.suffix/1676476083225.jpeg) Rules of Golf Rules Review: I thought my ball was lost and put another in play, then found my first in the hole(!) Which ball counts?](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/rules-review-ball-lost-replaced-but-actually-in-hole-which-ball-counts [link_37])

[![Image 3](https://golfdigest.sports.sndimg.com/content/dam/images/golfdigest/fullset/2023/1/rickie-fowler-dormant-bermuda-chip-american-express.jpg.rend.hgtvcom.406.271.suffix/1673478635254.jpeg) Chunk no more PGA Tour coach: 2 shots you need for 'the most daunting short game lie in golf'](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/short-game-chipping-wet-grainy-dormant-bermuda [link_38])

[![Image 4](https://golfdigest.sports.sndimg.com/content/dam/images/golfdigest/fullset/2021/230111-netflix-spieth-jt-th.png.rend.hgtvcom.406.406.suffix/1673460565875.png) Grab Your Popcorn Netflix finally drops first teaser (and release date) for new pro golf docuseries—and it looks fantastic](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/netflix-finally-drops-first-teaser-release-date-for-new-golf-show-full-swing-video [link_39])

But for pro golfers, two questions aren’t enough. The level of talent in professional golf is deeper than ever. Plenty of players post absurdly low scores on mini-tours, and while it’s widely conceded the PGA Tour has the most difficult setups, not all of the other tours' golf courses are pushovers. Yet should all those players be eligible for the Masters? Probably not.

Knowing that, the first deviation for the Pro Golf Handicap (PGH) would be the need for a deeper analysis of the golf courses, which I’m calling the Adjusted Course Rating (ACR). Remember, at the highest levels of golf, the layouts players must navigate in tournament play hardly resemble what an average player faces on normal weeks. Rough is higher, greens are faster, pins are tucked closer to the edges.

In a Pro Golf Handicap, there would need to be a course rating system that also factors in setup variables, which is to say, shooting 70 at Winged Foot from the tips is already damn good, but if you’re doing it under U.S. Open conditions, it’s elite. How would we arrive at this calculation? It could be a combination of factoring in fixed numbers—green speeds, rough height, distances of pins from collars—but also comparing the scores to the field average that day. Strokes-gained formulas are devised similarly, and the OWGR has one of those, too, but for reasons I’ll explain later, the OWGR’s strokes-gained metric is also problematic.

## Not just where, but when

So the Adjusted Course Rating is one unique requirement of a Pro Handicap. The other is admittedly even more complex, because as we know, a professional golfers’ performance is not just about what they shoot and where, but when. The significance of the tournament, what was at stake, whether they started the day with the lead or were 10 strokes back—this is another layer of context that contributes to a scores’ degree of difficulty. Again, if we agree there’s a difference between shooting 70 on different course setups, we can probably also agree there’s a difference between shooting 70 on Thursday morning of a Korn Ferry Tour event and Sunday evening of a U.S. Open. For this formula to work, it would require a combination of historical data (a final-round leader’s average score, etc) and other considerations that factor in a round’s specific challenge.

> The Professional Golf Handicap* = ([Adjusted Course Rating x Situational Difficulty Index] - 18-hole Tournament Score) ÷ Tournament Rounds

*As designed by an English major

Admittedly, this Situational Difficulty Index (SDI) requires some subjectivity to determine why one round of golf is more important than another, and it immediately raises the sticky question of what magnitude should be assigned to a tournament’s history or “prestige”* (which would presumably favor long-running PGA Tour or DP World Tour events over the inaugural LIV Golf events). So yes, some of this criteria will require real decisions by real people, but the goal is for the data to take over from there.

_(*There’s also the even murkier question of money. One might assume the more money at stake in an event the greater the magnitude, and in some cases that’s true. BUT … if a tour is throwing piles of money at players to begin with and even last place money is guaranteed and significant, one could argue the payout ceases to play a determining role.)_

So could this actually work? Could a Pro Handicap actually replace the OWGR as a fairer way of measuring one player against another? Here it’s important to remember the problem we’re trying to solve, and the reasons why the current system doesn’t do it. Beyond LIV Golf’s infamous source of funding, its detractors will say its competitive product is inferior, a tour seeking legitimacy by way of slapping a few zeroes at the end of tournament purses. In the absence of World Ranking points for its events, players who aren’t otherwise exempt for majors will slip further down the OWGR until they’re shut out altogether.

To which you might say, tough luck. This was the choice those players made when joining LIV. Maybe that’s true, but remember, the major championships are the most important events in golf because they bring the best players in the game together on the best courses. To exclude LIV golfers from competing jeopardizes that promise, in turn undermining the majors’ importance. This could be bad for golf.

So if we want the best players in golf eligible for the most important tournaments, then we need an apples-to-apples method to determine a player’s current level of play. The OWGR is currently reviewing LIV Golf’s application to award World Ranking points, but it appears that LIV tournaments won’t satisfy the OWGR requirements for inclusion and perhaps understandably. Winning a LIV Golf event—over just 54 holes, against a 48-man field—isn’t as demanding as a PGA Tour event played over 72 holes against 155 other players.

But shouldn’t those performances count for _something_? And if so, how?

The OWGR, and to an extent even [its own strokes-gained world rating](link_40), is more concerned with how golfers fare against one another than how they fare against the assortment of courses they play. The objective of a golf tournament is to win, of course, so winning would need to be rewarded in the PGHI formula. But the OWGR’s reliance on strength of field also makes it a self-fulfilling prophecy: a field’s strength is determined by the World Ranking of its players, which those players achieve by playing in events with strong fields. (Raise your hand if your head hurts.)

The Pro Handicap, meanwhile, eliminates most of the subjectivity of determining one tournament’s worth over another, and returns to the simpler questions of how well you play on these level of courses under these specific circumstances. Again, if the objective is to round up the most qualified golfers for the most important tournaments, this could do it.

If a LIV golfer not already exempt wants to prove why he deserves inclusion in the most important tournaments, the path to do so would be there. But that path is narrower for a reason. An Adjusted Course Rating would reflect LIV courses that are set up generally easier than those on the PGA Tour, and the Situational Difficulty Index would likely reveal most LIV tournament rounds by definition don’t present as steep a challenge. You’re playing against only 47 players, for starters, and since the formula gives greater weight to rounds as tournaments progress, LIV’s 54-hole format means its final round won’t be as “heavy” as the fourth round of a 72-hole event.

If you’ve read this far, it’s because you either think the Pro Handicap has real merit or because you think it’s so absurd you can’t look away. In fact both might be true. The Pro Handicap is indeed an imperfect system. But given the imperfect state of golf these days, and the imperfect system it endeavors to replace, it still might actually work.

 By [Tod Leonard](link_29)October 3, 2026

 Save for later 

Divider

**There seems to be little that happens quietly in Michael Block’s life.**

He is, after all, the most polarizing golf club pro on the planet, and he continues to make competitive waves on PGA Tour Champions. Block is once again contending for his first senior title this week in the Jefferson Lehigh Valley Classic, taking the clubhouse lead on Saturday by shooting 63. But he doesn’t need a victory to celebrate a big milestone, and that part has gone under the radar.

As [reported by the Daily Breeze](https://www.dailybreeze.com/2026/10/01/michael-block-to-secure-pga-tour-champions-membership-this-weekend/) in Orange County, Block will officially become a member of the over-50 circuit after Lehigh because he'll have made seven starts this season and has earnings that put him well into the top 72 on tour. Block has three top-10s since turning 50 in June and had earned $326,486. That would have put him at No. 50 in the Charles Schwab Cup standings as a member, and he figures to climb farther up with another strong result in Allentown, Pa. So, Block is in the three-event playoffs that begin Oct. 23 at the Stifel Charity Classic in St. Louis—which happens to be his hometown. Just one more crazy Blockie twist.

“I really didn’t think it was a possibility with such a short season left [after turning 50] that I could make the playoffs,” Block told Southland Golf, “but that was my goal—and now it’s going to happen. It’s unbelievable.”

# [The Tiger Vault Watch Series](link_29)

## Overview

Welcome to the Tiger Vault, where a lot of Golf Digest's exclusive Tiger Woods content is housed. Golf Digest's long-term creative partnership with Tiger has resulted in several premium video series produced by our team, from rare home visits and celebrity playing lessons to amateur swing roasts and one-on-one interviews about Tiger's tournaments and history in the game. Browse our existing series below and check back regularly for new additions!

# A cautionary tale for Tom Kim: This South Korean golf star served in the military and has never been the same

![Image 1: 2175044911](https://golfdigest.sports.sndimg.com/content/dam/images/golfdigest/fullset/2026/9/GettyImages-2175044911.jpg.rend.hgtvcom.966.644.suffix/1790109792371.jpeg)

Jared C. Tilton

By[Tod Leonard](https://www.golfdigest.com/contributor/tod-leonard)

 September 30, 2026 

Save for later

The Sunday of last week’s Presidents Cup had the potential to deliver one of the greatest moments of Tom Kim’s life. If his International team could build on the three-point lead it forged over the first three days at Medinah Country Club, he would have been the firebrand who led an enormous upset because his four points earned were the most for either team.

We’ve seen the excitable South Korean pump his fist, wave his arms and cup his hand to his ear in these competitions. Imagine what he’d do in a winning ceremony with a bottle of champagne in his hand. Remember the bubbly that comically shot out of captain Ian Woosnam’s nostrils at the 2006 Ryder Cup? Picture something like that.

Except that was never going to happen, even if the Internationals won (and we know that didn’t happen [after the Americans staged a willful comeback on Sunday](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/presidents-cup-2026-americans-win)). The point being, Kim didn’t get to mourn that loss with his teammates and would have missed the joy of a win because he had to be on an early evening flight out of Chicago to Japan.

Why would he possibly let an opportunity like that slip away? Because, in the scope of his life and career, there was a far more important task to tend to—one that could greatly affect his continued path in professional golf.

As first reported by the Associated Press on Saturday night of the Presidents Cup, Kim scheduled himself to leave the United States for Japan on Sunday so that he would have preparation time for the Asian Games that begin on Tuesday night (U.S. time). The games are held every four years and include golf for men and women.

For every male competing in the games, there is a prize more valuable than a medal: Event winners as either individuals or on teams become exempt from South Korea’s requirement that every able-bodied male serve for nearly two years in the military. The requirement has been in place since 1957, and men are expected to fulfill the service between the ages of 18 and 35.

The only other way for an athlete to forgo the service: win a gold, silver or bronze medal in the Olympics, and in Kim’s first appearance in 2024 in Paris, he tied for eighth.

Kim is only 24 and after a resurgent 2026 PGA Tour campaign in which he won the Genesis Scottish Open and finished 14th in the FedEx Cup, the last thing he wants is to get a letter in the mail from the government telling him he needs to report for service.

The scary thing is, it could happen, and there’s a cautionary tale for all Korean golfers in the sad case of Sangmoon Bae, a 16-time worldwide winner.

![Image 2: Albertsons Boise Open - Final Round](https://golfdigest.sports.sndimg.com/content/dam/images/golfdigest/fullset/2018/09/17/5b9f0918d13b8a2d32b268c2_GettyImages-1034553134.jpg.rend.hgtvcom.966.644.suffix/1573248557977.jpeg)

Sangmoon Bae celebrates winning Korn Ferry Tour Boise event in 2018.

Steve Dykes

In the early 2010s, Bae was among his country’s best professional players and rose to a career-high 26th in the world in 2011 with three victories that year in Asian events. He got on the PGA Tour in 2012 and only a year later won the Byron Nelson over runner-up Keegan Bradley. In 2014, he added another victory in the Frys.com Open and made the International Presidents Cup team in 2015. His was a career in full bloom.

But all of those accomplishments didn’t keep the South Korean government from telling Bae to report for duty, and after a court battle that he lost, he started his service in November 2015, only weeks after playing in the Presidents Cup, which the U.S. narrowly won, ironically enough, in South Korea.

"You know, I just hope I will play good when I come back," [Bae told Golf Digest in 2015](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/heres-why-you-should-root-for-sang-moon-bae-at-the-barclays-on-sunday). "Because I really love golf and playing on the PGA Tour."

Bae, who was 29 at the time, would serve 21 months in the South Korean army, with many of his fellow soldiers being a full decade younger than him. He was made a rifleman even though he’d never held a gun before he began his service, and he rarely had time to practice golf.

When he finally returned to professional golf late in 2017 at an Asian Tour event, Bae was blunt about his time spent away: "From the day when I was a private second class, a private first class and even the last day of the service, I wanted to be discharged from the military. I wanted to play in tournaments, I wanted to sleep at home and I wanted to drive."

The two years gone would prove devastating to Bae’s golf. When he left for the military, he was ranked 88th in the world; when he returned, he was 1,869th. And whatever competitive edge that Bae felt before his service, he lost it. Bae returned to the PGA Tour fulltime in 2017 and made only five of 17 cuts. Midway through that season, he lamented to the Associated Press, “I’ve kind of lost my feel how to play golf. Not how to swing—I forgot how to play golf.”

Remarkably, in one of only three starts in 2018 on the Korn Ferry Tour, Bae won in Boise, Idaho, but he lost his PGA Tour card after the 2018-19 season and has seen his chances to play in the States dwindle every year since. This season, he got a single start on the PGA Tour—in the Corales Puntacana Championship, in which he shot 77-75 to miss the cut.

Nearly all of Bae’s appearances this year have come in Asia, where he’s played 13 times across three tours and currently is on an unfortunate streak of five cuts missed. There was one promising finish for the now-40-year-old—a tie for third in the 68th Korean Open.

We will never know what Bae’s path would have been without the military duty, but we know this: It’s a road Tom Kim would very much like to avoid.

[Tod Leonard](https://www.golfdigest.com/contributor/tod-leonard)

Oct 3

**It’s probably not very generous to say that any score of 58 in pro golf should come with an asterisk. But we will anyway.**

Japan’s Yuta Suguira played tremendously well in the third round of the Korn Ferry Tour's Compliance Solutions Championship in Owasso, Okla., making 10 birdies and an eagle to shoot 12-under 58 at The Patriot Golf Club. It was the fourth sub-60 score in KFT history, and a bogey kept Suguira from tying the all-time mark of 57 set by Cristobal del Solar’in the 2024 Astara Golf Championship.

We give Suguira an enthusiastic golf clap instead of a throwing our fists in the air for several reasons. The KFT offers pushover courses at times, including the Patriot, which surrendered a 59 last year to Davis Chatfield while Adrien Dumont de Chassart opened with two 61s en route to a record-breaking total of 33 under. As with last year, it doesn’t help the course’s defense that the golfers are playing preferred lies. The scoring average for the round was a KFT-record 66.57, and there were two 60s, including William Sides lipping out a birdie putt on 18 for 59. Is this really the “test” you want in the first of two KFT Finals events?

For his work, Suguira—the 2025 Japan Tour rookie of the year—moved into a tie for eighth heading into Sunday. The leader at 21 under is Trent Phillips, who shot 61 on Saturday.

[Tod Leonard](https://www.golfdigest.com/contributor/tod-leonard)

Oct 3

**There seems to be little that happens quietly in Michael Block’s life.**

He is, after all, the most polarizing golf club pro on the planet, and he continues to make competitive waves on PGA Tour Champions. Block is once again contending for his first senior title this week in the Jefferson Lehigh Valley Classic, taking the clubhouse lead on Saturday by shooting 63. But he doesn’t need a victory to celebrate a big milestone, and that part has gone under the radar.

As [reported by the Daily Breeze](https://www.dailybreeze.com/2026/10/01/michael-block-to-secure-pga-tour-champions-membership-this-weekend/) in Orange County, Block will officially become a member of the over-50 circuit after Lehigh because he'll have made seven starts this season and has earnings that put him well into the top 72 on tour. Block has three top-10s since turning 50 in June and had earned $326,486. That would have put him at No. 50 in the Charles Schwab Cup standings as a member, and he figures to climb farther up with another strong result in Allentown, Pa. So, Block is in the three-event playoffs that begin Oct. 23 at the Stifel Charity Classic in St. Louis—which happens to be his hometown. Just one more crazy Blockie twist.

“I really didn’t think it was a possibility with such a short season left [after turning 50] that I could make the playoffs,” Block told Southland Golf, “but that was my goal—and now it’s going to happen. It’s unbelievable.”

Oct 2

**The Bank of Utah Championship kept arguably its biggest TV viewer and fan draw for the weekend, and Jackson Koivun made even that dramatic.**

Needing to rally to make the cut at the Black Desert Resort, the 21-year-old rookie birdied the 14th and 16th holes but still had to make at least a 4 on the 600-yard, par-5 finisher. And it didn’t look good when Koivun’s tee shot found a fairway bunker. “Didn't have the greatest lie," he recounted. "But I pulled 3-wood and I was, like, ‘I'm going to go for broke here.’ Came out nicely.”

Boy, did it. Koivun hammered that wood from the sand 260 yards and ended up just 43 yards from the flag. From there, clipped a low chip to five feet and made the birdie putt to shoot four-under 67 and finish on the cut number at six under. It's worth watching:

After earning 2½ points in Team USA's win last week, including a singles victory over Si Woo Kim, Koivun admitted on Friday to being “mentally exhausted” and “struggling with some emotions.” And for those reasons, he said, “I’m really proud of the way I fought back on those last nine holes.”

Oct 2

**Kevin Streelman has only two top-10 finishes in the past three years on the PGA Tour and the last of his two career victories came more than a decade ago—in 2014.**

So he was to be forgiven on Friday when he couldn’t remember the last time he’d played in the final group on a weekend. The subject came up because Streelman got into the final three-ball on Saturday for the third round of the Bank of Utah Championship. Guys have been shooting lights out amid the red rocks and black lava fields, and the 47-year-old Streelman went 63-64 to be two shots behind leader Austin Smotherman. Streelman wasn’t originally in the field but got in on his number when Lanto Griffin pulled out. “Very thankful and fortunate to be here. Also, I feel like I have nothing to lose, really,” Streelman said.

Streelman is the definition of a journeyman, having played 19 consecutive seasons on the tour, with 11 more appearances left to reach 500. He could only make 10 starts in 2025 after tearing the meniscus in his knee. “My family's coming in this weekend. I just feel I'm going to try and attack and have fun,” said Streelman, who is 151st in the FedEx Cup and could make a huge jump toward the top 100 with a strong finish.

Sep 26

**The lament in international team play if things don’t go well is, “We didn’t make enough putts.”**

How about when every putt seems to go in? The third match among Saturday’s fourball at Medinah featured some [predictable bombs by Canadian Nick Taylor](https://www.golfdigest.com/post/the-lament-in-international-team-play-if-things-don-t-go-well-is) on the greens. But the excitement among Americans fans is how the home team finally found somebody to match him. Cup rookie Chris Gotterup—spurned by Ryder Cup captain Keegan Bradley a year ago—went out of his mind with the flatstick on the back nine in a tight match playing alongside Cam Young against Taylor and Corey Conners.

Sparked by Young shooting five under, including concessions, over the first six holes, the Americans never trailed but were still only 2 up when Taylor did his stuff and drained a 50-footer for birdie at the 14th. It looked like the boost the Internationals needed, but then Gotterup topped him with a 50-footer of his own that produced a huge roar. On the very next hole, Gotterup came through again by making a 34-foot birdie to put the Americans 3 up, and after Taylor answered by making a 28-footer at 16, Gotterup rolled in yet another one, from 33 feet, to halve the hole and close out the match.

Clearly, a Presidents Cup putting duel to be remembered, and captain Brandt Snedeker, hoping to keep a hot hand, sent the pair out again in the afternoon foursomes. The original movie was going to be hard to top.

**If there's something the U.S. Presidents Cup team can hang its hat on as it trails 7-3 heading into Day 3, it's what the Americans did at Montreal.**

They overcame a Friday foursomes sweep by the Internationals by outscoring them 6-2 in Saturday’s two sessions to take a comfortable lead Since they trail by four points, 7-3, this time, they’ll need to set a strong tone early, and each captain has gone with some familiar duos.

[Coleman Bentley](https://www.golfdigest.com/contributor/coleman-bentley)

Oct 2

**Mama Fitzpatrick may have just hit the shot of the tournament.**

Despite [a breakout season](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/watch-alex-fitzpatrick-get-hit-with-delightful-dagger-from-dad-after-winning-first-pga-tour-title) for Alex Fitzpatrick and brother Matt enjoying what he called ["the best form of my life"](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/matt-fitzpatrick-s--best-form-of-my-life--continues-with-a-secon) leading up to the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship, it was their mom who hit the shot of the tournament on Friday. Playing alongside her sons in the pro-am, the Fitzpatrick matriach hit this ludicrous fairway metal to three feet, well inside of her PGA Tour-pro sons' respective approaches.

Not only was this an incredible shot and a fantastic family moment, but it was also a reminder for all us sons out there that no matter where life takes us, mom always knows best.

[](https://www.golfdigest.com/post/haotong-li-tells-masters-meltdown-story)

[Coleman Bentley](https://www.golfdigest.com/contributor/coleman-bentley)

Oct 1

**"That's a half mill there!"**

It's been six months since Haotong Li[crashed out of Masters contention](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/masters-2026-this-contender-may-have-just-played-the-worst-back-to-back-holes-in-masters-history) with a wild triple-bogey/quintuple-bogey Sunday meltdown at Augusta National. After finding Rae's Creek not once but twice on No. 12, Li goosed his approach on No. 13 long and into the bushes behind the green. It took Li three hacks to escape, before blasting his bogey putt off the green and into, you guessed it, Rae's Creek. Li, who was in the mix for a top-10 finish at the time of the implosion, shot a final-round 80 to finish in a tie for 38th.

This week, [Li joined the Life on Tour podcast](https://www.europeantour.com/dpworld-tour/news/podcast/haotong-li-growing-up-in-china-meeting-kevin-hart-at-the-masters-and-dancing-with-ernie-els/) and discussed the incident with his trademark candor, revealing it took him almost three whole days to understand the gravity what he had just done.

"I was like 'oh sh-t, that's actually really cost me a lot. That's half mill there!" Li said of his brutal realization. "Right after that day I couldn't feel anything. I was so numb. My mental … my whole body just numb. Literally until three days later, I was 'oh sh-t, this is not great!' [laughter]"

The good news is that Li is now able to laugh it off, but you know what they say: Sometimes you have to laugh to keep from crying.

Sep 29

**Bryson's lefty swing is absolutely filthy.**

Bryson DeChambeau is a shape shifter. He's assumed various roles throughout his career—[the scientist](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/bryson-dechambeau-says-hell-putt-with-the-pin-in-next-year-most-of-the-time-because-science), [the body builder](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/just-listening-to-bryson-dechambeau-s-daily-food-intake-will-mak), [the YouTube host](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/bryson-dechambeau-announces-return-of-hole-in-one-challenge)—carving out countless unforgettable moments, both good and bad, along the way. Now, we may be witsnessing of the birth south-paw Bryson after this video of him PIPING a drive lefty went viral on Tuesday.

Sheeeesh. That's one of the best switch-hitter swings we've seen since Mickey Mantle. Sure, his clubhead and ball speeds are noticeably slower, but as a result, his tempo actually seems smoother and sweeter. Almost Ernie Els-ish in its effortless arc. Keep hating all you want, but this is another point on the board for DeChambeau, who despite all his eccentricities, continues to prove he's one of the most multi-talented humans in all of golf.

[Coleman Bentley](https://www.golfdigest.com/contributor/coleman-bentley)

Sep 29

**So much for the element of surprise.**

It's been a big year for Wyndham Clark. He racked up three wins, including his second U.S. Open title, to put himself firmly in the PGA Tour Player of the Year conversation. More importantly, he's planning to propose to his girlfriend Emily Tanner after the Presidents Cup, a fact that he [accidentally blurted out](https://x.com/jamierkennedy/status/2092623853277081936) at East Lake last month. But don't worry, love birds, despite ruining the surprise, Clark told reporters that engagement is still very on following the U.S. team's comeback victory at Medinah on Sunday.

Asked if that premature reveal was a "slip up," Clark replied, "Kind of! When they [reporters] asked me what I was doing, that's what was on my mind because that's really all I'm focused on. So I said it and was like 'oh boy,' But she already knew—we went and picked out the rings and stuff ... but now I gotta really try to disguise when I'm going to do it."

So there you have it, folks. With a little luck, maybe Mr. and Mrs. Wyndham Clark will get to enjoy their honeymoon at Adare Manor next fall.

**Stop what you're doing and watch this filthy Jackson Koivun flop shot.**

It's been bumpy road for the Americans so far at Medinah, but one of the bright spots has been the play of 21-year-old phenom Jackson Koivun. Koivun looked nervous on Thursday, but more than found his feet during Saturday's four-ball session, carrying partner Justin Thomas with [one incredible shot](https://x.com/GolfChannel/status/2103866754426401020) after the next. The pick of the litter, however, was this effortless flop shot on the par-4 14th hole. Feast your eyes.

Almost everything about this shot, from the tight fairway lie to the pin tucked on the short side, looked like a nightmare. It would have been so easy to dump it in the bunker or thin it into the grandstands ... at least for us mere mortals. Instead, Koivun, cozied it up to five feet and even threw a little sauce on it, sheathing his wedge in one continuous motion from his follow through. Sick stuff, kid. Something tells us we'll be seeing you at Adare Manor next year.

**Brace yourselves, the Presidents Cup beer prices are here.**

On Tuesday, the [2026 Presidents Cup](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/presidents-cup-2026-power-rankings-for-all-24-players-at-medinah) got rolling as players and media arrived at Medinah for the 16th edition of the U.S. vs. Internationals event. The expectation is that there won't be a lot of intrigue on the course with the International team [having lost ten straight](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/presidents-cup-2026-what-happened-to-international-mens-golf-development) and once again playing sans LIV pros, but there's always plenty of drama in the concessions tent, where beer prices have become the talk of the gallery once again.

In contrast to the downright exploitative pricing we've seen at majors and Ryder Cups over the past decade, however, the buzz around the 2026 Presidents Cup beer prices is ... pretty good actually? In a sports world where $16 Bud Lights have become the rule not the exception, a Goose Island for $11.50 is a step in the right direction. If you're looking to pench some pennies (and calories), the Michelob Ultra clocks in at $10.50, which is not too far off what a gallon of gas will cost soon. So have heart, gallery goers. Maybe all our complaining has finally paid off.

**"Good shot again, Bob!"**

Ordinary golfers would give anything to have the ability of their professional counterparts. "If only I could hit a high draw like that, I could die happy," we've all thought while glued to the TV on a sunny Sunday afternoon.

The thing that makes golf so compelling, however, is that no matter skilled/rich/famous you get, perfection always lies just out of reach. Don't believe us? Just ask four-time DP World Tour winner Robert MacIntyre, who had some choice words for himself after missing the fairway on the par-4 1st at Wentworth on Friday. Sound up.

Of course, MacIntyre is better than 99 percent of golfers on earth, and a short while later he proved it, [holing out from the fairway for eagle](https://x.com/DPWorldTour/status/2100865607260381614) on No. 15 and backing that up with another superbird on No. 17. Still, it goes to show that there is no such as perfection or satisfaction in this game. All any of us can do—including our self-deprecating friend Mr. MacIntyre—is to keep on keeping on.

# The Passion of Jason Kelce

A retired football star invests time and money into golf his way

By[Michael Croley](https://www.golfdigest.com/contributor/michael-croley)

 September 29, 2026 

Save for later

Jason Kelce is normal. Sure, he’s 6-foot-3 and weighs 270 pounds (down from 295) and bound for the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Yes, he signed a podcast deal with his younger brother by 23 months, Travis, for nine figures. Perhaps you’ve heard of Travis’ wife, whose fame is so vast it has its own orbit, which has drawn the elder Kelce and his family into the orbit, too. Jason also owns a beer company, an apparel company, a small herd of cows in an organic beef venture and, as of last year, he’s an investor in Sullivan County Golf Club, two hours north of New York City.

But aside from all these things, he’s just like you and me. Case in point, he’s late for his tee time at Sullivan County, a scrappy little nine-holer that was rescued, in part, by golf writer Tom Coyne, who managed to coax Bill Murray and later Kelce into investing. After a redesign, the course’s new greens are still scruffy, the two-man maintenance crew doing the work of a dozen, but the property is rounding into form. The renovations to the restaurant, bar and pro shop, which don’t rely on Mother Nature’s cooperation, have come off splendidly. The white walls with pops of blue and modern furniture make the inside feel almost like a Crate & Barrel showroom.

That golf exists here at all is a testament to the game’s hold on our imaginations. The landscape of the Catskills has always been better suited to outdoor pastimes like hiking, hunting and fishing. Yet, this course has been in continuous operation since 1925. Its fairways carve into mountains that rise high above the greens and tilt with the grade of the hillsides they rest upon. You’ll find no pretense or top-100 aspirations here. This is just golf for those who love it. Jeans and a sweatshirt are just fine.

Like any other middle-aged man after a car ride—and one extra pop the night before—Kelce steps from the vehicle tentatively, as if crossing a crevasse, his hips and back   
 knotted from sitting and in need of a good stretch. He could invest in nearly anything and play golf anywhere, but he’s here.

![Image 8: /content/dam/images/golfdigest/fullset/2026/9/GD0927_FEAT_KELCE_04 copy.jpg](https://golfdigest.sports.sndimg.com/content/dam/images/golfdigest/fullset/2026/9/GD0927_FEAT_KELCE_04%20copy.jpg.rend.hgtvcom.966.1449.suffix/1788902124313.jpeg)

2/3 - 
Peter Yang

Kelce is only two years removed from his football career. It’s not hard to picture him still wearing his Philadelphia Eagles uniform darkened by sweat, his cheeks pinched by his helmet, the cold air biting at his bare arms, but the brute’s demeanor on the range is docile. He pushes a handful of balls toward me, encouraging me to take a few swings, too. His game is a work in progress, just as it is for the rest of us.

“Every time I get my driver fixed up, then all of a sudden I can’t hit my irons, or I can’t chip. Then I’ll put a bunch of time into chipping, and then I’m terrible off the tee.” Today, he’s fighting the driver so much that he never takes its headcover off, opting instead for his mini-driver, which he can bust about 280 with just a slight tail of fade.

His entourage is five. There’s the head of his family office and business affairs, his security guy, an attaché who is a Mr. Fix-It, his longtime agent Jason Bernstein and Alejandro Villanueva, a former player for the Steelers. The group feels less like Kelce, Inc., than a collection of friends who’ve known him for a long time. Before we head out to play, we grab beers from the clubhouse (Garage Beers, of course, Kelce’s company) and tee off as a sixsome.

Kelce quickly sets up a side-game with Bernstein for a hundred bucks, steps to the first tee and booms the mini about a hundred yards short of the green. From far behind, Bernstein puts his approach pin-high just off the putting surface. Kelce fats his. On the cart ride to his third, Kelce laments the strike. Bernstein hits a good chip. When Kelce’s putt to tie Bernstein misses, Kelce lets out a thunderous F-bomb. The sound jolts everyone to attention, and the temperature of the air changes. Kelce’s eyes narrow, and his enormous chest swells somehow bigger. Wry smiles from his crew tell me this is a familiar story. No matter how genial their friend might be, he is a very competitive human being.

![Image 9: /content/dam/images/golfdigest/fullset/2026/9/GD0927_FEAT_KELCE_02 copy.jpg](https://golfdigest.sports.sndimg.com/content/dam/images/golfdigest/fullset/2026/9/GD0927_FEAT_KELCE_02%20copy.jpg.rend.hgtvcom.966.644.suffix/1788902122362.jpeg)

**LONG SNAPPER:** Expanded views at Sullivan County frame a Kelce pitch shot.

Peter Yang

When I ask Kelce why he has invested in Sullivan County Golf Club, he says he was drawn to its reclamation story after meeting Coyne as a guest on The Golfer’s Journal podcast. He appreciated what Coyne was trying to do and what public courses like this can mean to the game. As a kid, Kelce and his brother played regularly at Highland Park on the east side of Cleveland, where their father dropped them off with second-hand clubs from Play it Again Sports. (“Most of our sports equipment came from there.”) Kelce is pretty sure his father was using the course as a de facto babysitter. As he has taken up the game anew and played more in retirement, he sees the importance of these venues. “There’s a lot of people that view golf as a rich person’s game, and that is a very true aspect of it. But there’s also this other aspect of what’s happening in golf at courses like this, municipal courses, and courses I grew up on that is not that. The breadth of people and individuals from all walks of life that play the game is great. Whenever you have something that unites people from all different walks of life, that’s kind of where I like to be.”

Kelce’s post-football career was supposed to be quieter. While he was always going to be involved in investments and business deals—he wasn’t going to spend his days in a rocking chair—the calculus of it all changed when Kelce became mega famous the year before he retired. The Amazon documentary “Kelce” about the brothers probably raised his profile enough to put Monday Night Football commentating in the offing. Then a month before he and Travis inked the “New Heights” podcast with Amazon’s Wondery audio network, Travis and Taylor Swift went public that they were dating.

The other seminal moment that made Kelce a household name was the week after the Eagles were eliminated from the NFL playoffs in 2024. Jason traveled to Buffalo with his wife, Kylie, who has her own popular podcast, “Not Gonna Lie With Kylie Kelce,” to watch Travis in the playoffs with Swift in tow. The broadcast that winter day was repeatedly drawn to a shirtless Jason Kelce, ripping beers and screaming in ecstasy. At one point, he left the open window of the suite to fetch a young girl with a Swift sign to the box. Kylie’s voice could be heard over and over imploring him to return. A very public everyman and pitchman was born.

Between then and now, Kelce has become perhaps the most famous offensive lineman of all time, a position often relegated to anonymity. He has hosted a late-night show on ESPN and pitched dozens of products outside of his own companies. For a time, he was seemingly everywhere. Not quite Swiftian but similarly, almost everything he does is a news event. Just before we played golf, there was a dustup over comments he made regarding the NFL having too many games that weren’t played on Sundays. When I ask him how it feels to make news every time he speaks and about those comments specifically, he says, “I thought it was a pretty soft comment. I was just saying they might want to be careful because Sunday is an important day in football.” Regarding his fame he is sanguine, understanding how it can be utilized. “The whole goal of the comment is to create a conversation around it. Our family has had a heightened awareness on that, and a lot of that’s because of the fan base that has been built, obviously, in my own career, Travis’s career, and who Travis is about to marry, right?”

If there is a price to pay for such exposure, it’s the inevitable moments of backlash. That came harshest for Jason Kelce after his appearance at the 2026 Masters Par 3 Contest, where much of the online chatter was critical of his presence. When I bring it up, Kelce cuts me off, shouting in mock enthusiasm, “Shrink the game, baby!” He believes many misunderstood the purpose of his presence there, which was to be jovial and celebrate golf and the way the game is evolving.

Asked to be at the event by his employers at ESPN as well as the green jackets of Augusta National Golf Club, Kelce says he was very mindful of the stage he was walking onto. “A lot of people don’t want to see the tradition of Augusta and what it has meant changed. I don’t think we really did anything that drastically different, but I do understand the pushback because I think the game of golf is so rooted in tradition and history,” Kelce says, though he is also quick to assert that golf is different now, and can recite some of the hard supporting data. For example, the National Golf Foundation reports that golf participation is up 41 percent over the past six years and is approaching 50 million golfers. More anecdotally, the number of hats at premier golf resorts missing vowels or with backward printing point to new entrants with new attitudes.

“Golf is probably changing more now than it ever has,” Kelce says, “It’s growing, which causes a lot of that change, and I think it’s very natural when there’s so much growth and change happening, especially if it’s something you’ve loved and done your whole life, to want to keep that thing the way it is.”

About that tee shot he hit during the Par 3, Kelce first says, “Being respectful was my main goal.” When the opportunity to do so was first presented, he didn’t know if he would take the shot, but the desire was there. When he ultimately did take the shot, he says he was so nervous his back was shaking. “I’ve felt my knees shake. I’ve felt my ankles shake. I didn’t know your midsection could shake.”

![Image 10: 2270447379](https://golfdigest.sports.sndimg.com/content/dam/images/golfdigest/fullset/2026/2/GettyImages-2270447379.jpg.rend.hgtvcom.966.644.suffix/1788902321317.jpeg)

**MASTERS MOMENT:** Jason Kelce, broadcaster for ESPN, walks the course during the 2026 Par 3 Contest at Augusta National.

Hector Vivas

Leif Edgar, who works with Kelce’s family office and has known him since their college days at the University of Cincinnati, says the better memory of the 2026 Masters was when a high school volunteer came up to Kelce near Amen Corner to tell him he was a fan and that he was an offensive lineman, too. “Five minutes later, Jason is down in a three-point stance and showing this kid how to come off the line and get leverage over his opponent.”

Kelce loves to have a great time. He’ll drink beers shirtless at a winter playoff game or beat Neal Shipley in a chugging contest (by a good five seconds) during a TGL match, but away from the cameras, he slows down and is thoughtful and considerate. Several of his college friends I spoke with say the duality of his personality was always there, that deep conversations are as much a part of what he lives for as relaxing with a few beers. In high school, he attended an outdoors camp near Shaker Lakes and was often content to just sit beside a tree, drawing or writing in a journal. His business investments are driven by his interests. Profit isn’t the primary motivation in any, just a bonus. His apparel company, Underdog, takes its name from his speech after the Eagles won the Super Bowl in 2018 in which he declared “Underdogs are hungry dogs.” The clothing is manufactured in the United States and, Kelce says, is about honoring the diligence and dignity of work. “We obviously want to grow and make money, but we also want to do things that have a sense of purpose and meaning.”

> Not quite Swiftian but similarly, almost everything Kelce does is a news event.

During the photoshoot for this story, as Kelce poured Garage Beers from the tap, a new keg offered nothing but pints of foam. When I kidded him later that if all of America could see his pour technique, he’d lose a lot of credibility. He played along, aghast. “What was that?!” At turns jocular and reflective, Kelce comes across as self-aware and doesn’t take himself or his image too seriously.

Various employees came up to introduce themselves to him, and with each Kelce was gracious, thanking them for their work and their time. He did the same with a few golfers who wandered over after their rounds to also thank him for his investment. That Kelce feels he is investing in people really is what makes Sullivan County fit into his portfolio, a word he wouldn’t use. “A big reason I invested here is this relationship I have with Tom, and I think that the story here and what he was doing individually caused that investment to happen.”

He and Travis have a theory that your personality will determine your playing position. Travis, as more of an artist, drifted toward receiving and has a sense of improvisation when he plays. Jason is much more analytical, which suits the position of center. “I think it’s no coincidence that we ended up playing the positions we did. At center you have to be very prepared and think about all the possible outcomes that can happen leading up to the game. What will this call do? How will that affect the attack? Will this happen? How does that affect the running back or the quarterback? No surprise I ended up on the offensive line.”

**Tom Kim is close to a potential military exemption at the Asian Games.**

There are two ways for a South Korean golfer to get an exemption from the military service that is otherwise mandatory for male citizens between ages 18 and 35. You can win an Olympic medal, or you can take gold in the individual or team event at the Asian Games. This week in Japan, Tom Kim is attempting the latter, and after two rounds at the Kasugai Country Club East Course, he's [exactly where he stood](https://results.asiangames2026.org/#/discipline/GLF/results/M.STROKE------------.FNL-.000300--) at the end of Round 1: Two shots off the lead, now held by both Wenyi Ding and Wei-hsuan Wang. Kim shot 66 in the second round, and as a team the Koreans are in solo third at a collective 14 under, trailing the leaders Japan by just two shots. As Tod Leonard [covered](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/tom-kim-south-korea-military-service-asian-games-sangmoo-bae) here at Digest, the stakes are high—compulsory military service takes between 18 and 21 months, time for practicing golf is scarce, and players like Sangmoon Bae were never quite the same after serving. At 24, Kim could have another shot at the 2028 Olympics or the 2023 Asian Games, but even that is uncertain, as Bae had to begin his service at age 29. Two rounds remain at this year's Asian Games.

**Great Britain & Ireland's greatest hope to end their Walker Cup drought might be a stomach bug.**

Starting Saturday, the 51st Walker Cup will kick off at Lahinch Golf Club in Ireland, and the home team, Great Britain & Ireland, will be trying to win for the first time since 2015. Earlier, our Jamie Kennedy [explored](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/2026-walker-cup--is-lahinch-the-home-field-advantage-gb-i-need-t) whether the Irish course will give them the advantage they need, but now they seem to have a new ally: A stomach bug. According to Golf Channel's Brentley Romine, illness [kept two American players from practicing on Thursday](https://www.golfchannel.com/ncaa/news/multiple-u-s-walker-cuppers-miss-thursday-practice-with-stomach-issues), Oklahoma State's Ethan Fang and Alabama's William Jennings. The U.S. captain, Nathan Smith, said they're "good to go," but then again, that's what you would say, isn't it? As Romine noted, this seems to be a common theme: a stomach bug hit 16 different players at the 2021 Walker Cup, requiring alternates to swap in, and some players had to visit the ER. And at the Rome Ryder Cup in 2023, members of the American team contracted a mysterious illness before enduring a thumping from Europe. Hopefully, for the sake of competition, everybody will be ready to play at Lahinch on Saturday, but now the Americans have a built-in excuse if things go wrong for the first time in a decade.

**It's Friday afternoon, and Jacob Bridgeman just hit his ball into a pizza tent.**

Folks, we don't mean to shock you out of your senses before the weekend, but a player on the PGA Tour just sprayed the hell out of his tee shot, it ended up in a pizza tent and—I hope you're sitting down—it was not Jordan Spieth. The player was Jacob Bridgeman, it happened on the 18th hole, and you can tell it wasn't Spieth because instead of playing the ball from under the counter and making a miracle par, Bridgeman took the drop and made bogey. He finished at 5 under, and sits at T-14 after 36 holes in Atlanta. You can watch the result in the tweet below, but first, I am contractually obligated to say the following: Now that's what I call a slice!

**When it comes to the tour's new match-play finale format, you heard it here first (no, seriously).**

Earlier Tuesday morning, Brian Rolapp [announced](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/pga-tour-reimagined-finish-to-tour-season-in-2028-includes-two-week-match-play-postseason-event) that starting in 2028, the Tour Championship would be contested as a 32-man, two-week match-play event. That's great news for the match-play fans, but when it came to the 16-person final weekend, it also sounded pretty familiar. That's because the central concept, of all 16 players playing all four match-play sessions, was something proposed on [these very pages back in 2024](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/pga-tour-championship-fixes-changes-fedex-cup-playoffs-golfpocalypse) (skip to point 3). And, as you see below, we reprised it for a social video last summer (1:50 mark). The exact details of how it will work aren't yet 100 percent clear, but it seems likely that the format of the last four rounds is a clone. That just proves the tour has great taste. All we ask in return is that Golf Digest be named the title sponsor of the Tour Championship at no cost, and for me personally to be paid $1 million. That's fair, right?

**Jim Furyk says there's a new U.S. Ryder Cup qualification system coming.**

Ten days ago, Europe [announced its qualifying system](https://www.golfdigest.com/story/ryder-cup-team-europe-qualification-2027-adare-manor-luke-donald) for the 2027 Ryder Cup at Adare Manor, and as befits a team who piles on success after success, it looks basically the same as 2025 … and 2023. Today, U.S. captain Jim Furyk told [Golfweek](https://golfweek.usatoday.com/story/sports/golf/ryder-cup/2026/08/14/us-ryder-cup-team-new-qualification-rules-2027-adare-manor/91303102007/) that America's system will be announced after this year's FedEx Cup playoffs, but that unlike the Europeans, big changes are afoot. There's not much information yet, but apparently the change will skew toward valuing events that take place in 2027, which means it could end up looking like the European system, which has always put far less emphasis (read: none) on off-year majors. The only American who won a major this year was Wyndham Clark, so in theory this is bad news for him. “It’s going to be the right way to identify the best six players in September 2027," Furyk said.

Divider

**There seems to be little that happens quietly in Michael Block’s life.**

He is, after all, the most polarizing golf club pro on the planet, and he continues to make competitive waves on PGA Tour Champions. Block is once again contending for his first senior title this week in the Jefferson Lehigh Valley Classic, taking the clubhouse lead on Saturday by shooting 63. But he doesn’t need a victory to celebrate a big milestone, and that part has gone under the radar.

As [reported by the Daily Breeze](https://www.dailybreeze.com/2026/10/01/michael-block-to-secure-pga-tour-champions-membership-this-weekend/) in Orange County, Block will officially become a member of the over-50 circuit after Lehigh because he'll have made seven starts this season and has earnings that put him well into the top 72 on tour. Block has three top-10s since turning 50 in June and had earned $326,486. That would have put him at No. 50 in the Charles Schwab Cup standings as a member, and he figures to climb farther up with another strong result in Allentown, Pa. So, Block is in the three-event playoffs that begin Oct. 23 at the Stifel Charity Classic in St. Louis—which happens to be his hometown. Just one more crazy Blockie twist.

“I really didn’t think it was a possibility with such a short season left [after turning 50] that I could make the playoffs,” Block told Southland Golf, “but that was my goal—and now it’s going to happen. It’s unbelievable.”

# The Passion of Jason Kelce

A retired football star invests time and money into golf his way

By[Michael Croley](https://www.golfdigest.com/contributor/michael-croley)

 September 29, 2026 

Save for later

Jason Kelce is normal. Sure, he’s 6-foot-3 and weighs 270 pounds (down from 295) and bound for the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Yes, he signed a podcast deal with his younger brother by 23 months, Travis, for nine figures. Perhaps you’ve heard of Travis’ wife, whose fame is so vast it has its own orbit, which has drawn the elder Kelce and his family into the orbit, too. Jason also owns a beer company, an apparel company, a small herd of cows in an organic beef venture and, as of last year, he’s an investor in Sullivan County Golf Club, two hours north of New York City.

But aside from all these things, he’s just like you and me. Case in point, he’s late for his tee time at Sullivan County, a scrappy little nine-holer that was rescued, in part, by golf writer Tom Coyne, who managed to coax Bill Murray and later Kelce into investing. After a redesign, the course’s new greens are still scruffy, the two-man maintenance crew doing the work of a dozen, but the property is rounding into form. The renovations to the restaurant, bar and pro shop, which don’t rely on Mother Nature’s cooperation, have come off splendidly. The white walls with pops of blue and modern furniture make the inside feel almost like a Crate & Barrel showroom.

That golf exists here at all is a testament to the game’s hold on our imaginations. The landscape of the Catskills has always been better suited to outdoor pastimes like hiking, hunting and fishing. Yet, this course has been in continuous operation since 1925. Its fairways carve into mountains that rise high above the greens and tilt with the grade of the hillsides they rest upon. You’ll find no pretense or top-100 aspirations here. This is just golf for those who love it. Jeans and a sweatshirt are just fine.

Like any other middle-aged man after a car ride—and one extra pop the night before—Kelce steps from the vehicle tentatively, as if crossing a crevasse, his hips and back   
 knotted from sitting and in need of a good stretch. He could invest in nearly anything and play golf anywhere, but he’s here.

Peter Yang

Kelce is only two years removed from his football career. It’s not hard to picture him still wearing his Philadelphia Eagles uniform darkened by sweat, his cheeks pinched by his helmet, the cold air biting at his bare arms, but the brute’s demeanor on the range is docile. He pushes a handful of balls toward me, encouraging me to take a few swings, too. His game is a work in progress, just as it is for the rest of us.

“Every time I get my driver fixed up, then all of a sudden I can’t hit my irons, or I can’t chip. Then I’ll put a bunch of time into chipping, and then I’m terrible off the tee.” Today, he’s fighting the driver so much that he never takes its headcover off, opting instead for his mini-driver, which he can bust about 280 with just a slight tail of fade.

His entourage is five. There’s the head of his family office and business affairs, his security guy, an attaché who is a Mr. Fix-It, his longtime agent Jason Bernstein and Alejandro Villanueva, a former player for the Steelers. The group feels less like Kelce, Inc., than a collection of friends who’ve known him for a long time. Before we head out to play, we grab beers from the clubhouse (Garage Beers, of course, Kelce’s company) and tee off as a sixsome.

Kelce quickly sets up a side-game with Bernstein for a hundred bucks, steps to the first tee and booms the mini about a hundred yards short of the green. From far behind, Bernstein puts his approach pin-high just off the putting surface. Kelce fats his. On the cart ride to his third, Kelce laments the strike. Bernstein hits a good chip. When Kelce’s putt to tie Bernstein misses, Kelce lets out a thunderous F-bomb. The sound jolts everyone to attention, and the temperature of the air changes. Kelce’s eyes narrow, and his enormous chest swells somehow bigger. Wry smiles from his crew tell me this is a familiar story. No matter how genial their friend might be, he is a very competitive human being.

![Image 9: /content/dam/images/golfdigest/fullset/2026/9/GD0927_FEAT_KELCE_02 copy.jpg](https://golfdigest.sports.sndimg.com/content/dam/images/golfdigest/fullset/2026/9/GD0927_FEAT_KELCE_02%20copy.jpg.rend.hgtvcom.966.644.suffix/1788902122362.jpeg)

**LONG SNAPPER:** Expanded views at Sullivan County frame a Kelce pitch shot.

Peter Yang

When I ask Kelce why he has invested in Sullivan County Golf Club, he says he was drawn to its reclamation story after meeting Coyne as a guest on The Golfer’s Journal podcast. He appreciated what Coyne was trying to do and what public courses like this can mean to the game. As a kid, Kelce and his brother played regularly at Highland Park on the east side of Cleveland, where their father dropped them off with second-hand clubs from Play it Again Sports. (“Most of our sports equipment came from there.”) Kelce is pretty sure his father was using the course as a de facto babysitter. As he has taken up the game anew and played more in retirement, he sees the importance of these venues. “There’s a lot of people that view golf as a rich person’s game, and that is a very true aspect of it. But there’s also this other aspect of what’s happening in golf at courses like this, municipal courses, and courses I grew up on that is not that. The breadth of people and individuals from all walks of life that play the game is great. Whenever you have something that unites people from all different walks of life, that’s kind of where I like to be.”

Kelce’s post-football career was supposed to be quieter. While he was always going to be involved in investments and business deals—he wasn’t going to spend his days in a rocking chair—the calculus of it all changed when Kelce became mega famous the year before he retired. The Amazon documentary “Kelce” about the brothers probably raised his profile enough to put Monday Night Football commentating in the offing. Then a month before he and Travis inked the “New Heights” podcast with Amazon’s Wondery audio network, Travis and Taylor Swift went public that they were dating.

The other seminal moment that made Kelce a household name was the week after the Eagles were eliminated from the NFL playoffs in 2024. Jason traveled to Buffalo with his wife, Kylie, who has her own popular podcast, “Not Gonna Lie With Kylie Kelce,” to watch Travis in the playoffs with Swift in tow. The broadcast that winter day was repeatedly drawn to a shirtless Jason Kelce, ripping beers and screaming in ecstasy. At one point, he left the open window of the suite to fetch a young girl with a Swift sign to the box. Kylie’s voice could be heard over and over imploring him to return. A very public everyman and pitchman was born.

Between then and now, Kelce has become perhaps the most famous offensive lineman of all time, a position often relegated to anonymity. He has hosted a late-night show on ESPN and pitched dozens of products outside of his own companies. For a time, he was seemingly everywhere. Not quite Swiftian but similarly, almost everything he does is a news event. Just before we played golf, there was a dustup over comments he made regarding the NFL having too many games that weren’t played on Sundays. When I ask him how it feels to make news every time he speaks and about those comments specifically, he says, “I thought it was a pretty soft comment. I was just saying they might want to be careful because Sunday is an important day in football.” Regarding his fame he is sanguine, understanding how it can be utilized. “The whole goal of the comment is to create a conversation around it. Our family has had a heightened awareness on that, and a lot of that’s because of the fan base that has been built, obviously, in my own career, Travis’s career, and who Travis is about to marry, right?”

If there is a price to pay for such exposure, it’s the inevitable moments of backlash. That came harshest for Jason Kelce after his appearance at the 2026 Masters Par 3 Contest, where much of the online chatter was critical of his presence. When I bring it up, Kelce cuts me off, shouting in mock enthusiasm, “Shrink the game, baby!” He believes many misunderstood the purpose of his presence there, which was to be jovial and celebrate golf and the way the game is evolving.

Asked to be at the event by his employers at ESPN as well as the green jackets of Augusta National Golf Club, Kelce says he was very mindful of the stage he was walking onto. “A lot of people don’t want to see the tradition of Augusta and what it has meant changed. I don’t think we really did anything that drastically different, but I do understand the pushback because I think the game of golf is so rooted in tradition and history,” Kelce says, though he is also quick to assert that golf is different now, and can recite some of the hard supporting data. For example, the National Golf Foundation reports that golf participation is up 41 percent over the past six years and is approaching 50 million golfers. More anecdotally, the number of hats at premier golf resorts missing vowels or with backward printing point to new entrants with new attitudes.

“Golf is probably changing more now than it ever has,” Kelce says, “It’s growing, which causes a lot of that change, and I think it’s very natural when there’s so much growth and change happening, especially if it’s something you’ve loved and done your whole life, to want to keep that thing the way it is.”

About that tee shot he hit during the Par 3, Kelce first says, “Being respectful was my main goal.” When the opportunity to do so was first presented, he didn’t know if he would take the shot, but the desire was there. When he ultimately did take the shot, he says he was so nervous his back was shaking. “I’ve felt my knees shake. I’ve felt my ankles shake. I didn’t know your midsection could shake.”

![Image 10: 2270447379](https://golfdigest.sports.sndimg.com/content/dam/images/golfdigest/fullset/2026/2/GettyImages-2270447379.jpg.rend.hgtvcom.966.644.suffix/1788902321317.jpeg)

**MASTERS MOMENT:** Jason Kelce, broadcaster for ESPN, walks the course during the 2026 Par 3 Contest at Augusta National.

Hector Vivas

Leif Edgar, who works with Kelce’s family office and has known him since their college days at the University of Cincinnati, says the better memory of the 2026 Masters was when a high school volunteer came up to Kelce near Amen Corner to tell him he was a fan and that he was an offensive lineman, too. “Five minutes later, Jason is down in a three-point stance and showing this kid how to come off the line and get leverage over his opponent.”

Kelce loves to have a great time. He’ll drink beers shirtless at a winter playoff game or beat Neal Shipley in a chugging contest (by a good five seconds) during a TGL match, but away from the cameras, he slows down and is thoughtful and considerate. Several of his college friends I spoke with say the duality of his personality was always there, that deep conversations are as much a part of what he lives for as relaxing with a few beers. In high school, he attended an outdoors camp near Shaker Lakes and was often content to just sit beside a tree, drawing or writing in a journal. His business investments are driven by his interests. Profit isn’t the primary motivation in any, just a bonus. His apparel company, Underdog, takes its name from his speech after the Eagles won the Super Bowl in 2018 in which he declared “Underdogs are hungry dogs.” The clothing is manufactured in the United States and, Kelce says, is about honoring the diligence and dignity of work. “We obviously want to grow and make money, but we also want to do things that have a sense of purpose and meaning.”

> Not quite Swiftian but similarly, almost everything Kelce does is a news event.

During the photoshoot for this story, as Kelce poured Garage Beers from the tap, a new keg offered nothing but pints of foam. When I kidded him later that if all of America could see his pour technique, he’d lose a lot of credibility. He played along, aghast. “What was that?!” At turns jocular and reflective, Kelce comes across as self-aware and doesn’t take himself or his image too seriously.

Various employees came up to introduce themselves to him, and with each Kelce was gracious, thanking them for their work and their time. He did the same with a few golfers who wandered over after their rounds to also thank him for his investment. That Kelce feels he is investing in people really is what makes Sullivan County fit into his portfolio, a word he wouldn’t use. “A big reason I invested here is this relationship I have with Tom, and I think that the story here and what he was doing individually caused that investment to happen.”

He and Travis have a theory that your personality will determine your playing position. Travis, as more of an artist, drifted toward receiving and has a sense of improvisation when he plays. Jason is much more analytical, which suits the position of center. “I think it’s no coincidence that we ended up playing the positions we did. At center you have to be very prepared and think about all the possible outcomes that can happen leading up to the game. What will this call do? How will that affect the attack? Will this happen? How does that affect the running back or the quarterback? No surprise I ended up on the offensive line.”

When asked how that impacts his golf, Jason concedes, “Thinking is not always better with this game.” At Rolling Green Golf Club in Springfield, Pa., where he holds an annual charity event, he once shot 100 with a 13 on one hole. “I went from bunker to bunker to bunker.” This past summer in Tahoe, at the American Century Celebrity Championship, Jason bet and lost to Travis over who would dress as a member of the Blue Man Group on their podcast.

![Image 11: /content/dam/images/golfdigest/fullset/2026/9/GD0927_FEAT_KELCE_06 copy.jpg](https://golfdigest.sports.sndimg.com/content/dam/images/golfdigest/fullset/2026/9/GD0927_FEAT_KELCE_06%20copy.jpg.rend.hgtvcom.966.1449.suffix/1788909815996.jpeg)

**CLUB MAN:** Hanging inside the clubhouse where the tournament boards date to the 1930s.

Peter Yang

For all Jason’s everyman bona fides, his love of a good time and being one of the guys, on the golf course he also comes across as someone who approaches every facet of life with a goal in mind. When he addresses the ball, a field of concentration envelops him, reminding us he wasn’t just a professional athlete but one of the best, someone who worked incredibly hard at his position and sport. Before each strike, Kelce disappears into his own world. After playing golf only sporadically during his football career, he has now gone down Reddit rabbit holes related to golf, asking strangers to fix his swing. He even had a driver made to Bryson DeChambeau’s specs, thinking it would help him, but admits, “I can’t hit that thing. It’s atrocious.” As for the lucrative podcast, which features a fair amount of golf talk, he rewatches and analyzes episodes the way he used to watch game film, too.

As for the match between Kelce and Bernstein, crisp shots punctuated by birdies is not the rule of the day. But it has been back and forth.

As we come to the ninth tee, Kelce is down one. It is a longish par 4 up a slight hill. Kelce puts a drive on the right side of the fairway, giving him an opening by an old stonewall. He executes a perfect 54-degree wedge to 10 feet. Bernstein, a hundred pounds lighter and five inches shorter, has repeatedly stormed back each time Kelce has pushed an advantage. It’s highly apparent how much he wants to beat the big man. Bernstein also finds the green. The putters will decide.

> ‘At center you have to be very prepared and think about all the possible outcomes ... Thinking is not always better with [golf].’

The greens are as slow as a shag carpet. No one has run one past all day. Predictably, Bernstein leaves it short. Before the round, Bernstein, Kelce’s agent for his entire career, told me that what has always made Jason special is not just his intellect and ability to work, but his focus.

“In what people would consider pressure moments, he’s focused and calm, and that extends beyond sports competition,” Bernstein says. “When he’s in front of an audience doing a live show or speaking, he is just locked in and performs his best.”

Of course, Kelce steps up and drains it. We clap as if he’s won the U.S. Open.

A debate about settling the tie with a chipping contest or a putting contest ensues, and I think, surely, they want to get on with it because of the event Kelce needs to attend at home in Philadelphia in the evening. But then I also remember Kelce has his own plane waiting at the local airstrip, something that is decidedly not like the rest of us.

Kelce declares they must play one more hole, so off to the first we go. Kelce is left with his usual 100 yards out. Bernstein hits his approach well short and fears it has plunged into a hidden creek short of the green.

Bernstein is peering into the water. Kelce is on his knees, wedge in hand, sliding the club’s face under the ball, steady as a bomb technician, fishing it out and placing it on dry land. He stands, mildly triumphant. Affording the ball isn’t the point, of course; it’s savoring the challenge. Bernstein’s drop and chip fail to make magic. Kelce chips on and has a five-footer for par to win. He fist-pumps as the ball disappears into the hole and makes an assured stride to retrieve the ball. He is a man used to victory, especially these days, but it still feels good, no matter how small, no matter where it takes place.
