The native form of this [personal name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_name "Personal name") is _Matsuyama Hideki_.This article uses [Western name order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_name#Western_name_order_(family_name_last) "Personal name") when mentioning individuals.

**Hideki Matsuyama** ([Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"): 松山 英樹, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Japanese "Romanization of Japanese"):_Matsuyama Hideki_; IPA:[[ma̠t͡sɨja̠ma̠çide̞kʲi]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Japanese "Help:IPA/Japanese"); born 25 February 1992) is a Japanese [professional golfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_golfer "Professional golfer") who plays on the [PGA Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGA_Tour "PGA Tour"). He is the first Japanese golfer to win a [men's major golf championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men's_major_golf_championships "Men's major golf championships")– the [2021 Masters Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Masters_Tournament "2021 Masters Tournament").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-shipnuck-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-pgatour-3)

As of January 2025, Matsuyama has 20 worldwide wins, an Olympic bronze medal, ten career top-10 finishes in major championships, and six [Presidents Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidents_Cup "Presidents Cup") appearances. Matsuyama is a two-time winner of tournaments in the [World Golf Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Golf_Championships "World Golf Championships"), two-time winner of the [Waste Management Phoenix Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waste_Management_Phoenix_Open "Waste Management Phoenix Open"), eight-time [Japan Golf Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Golf_Tour "Japan Golf Tour") winner, two-time winner of the [Asian Amateur Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_Amateur_Championship "Asian Amateur Championship"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-beall-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-history-5) and most recently winner of the [FedEx St. Jude Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FedEx_St._Jude_Championship "FedEx St. Jude Championship").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-genesis-6) His 11 wins on the [PGA Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGA_Tour "PGA Tour") make him the most successful Japanese member of the PGA Tour in history.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-beall-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-history-5)

Matsuyama was ranked first in the [World Amateur Golf Ranking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Amateur_Golf_Ranking "World Amateur Golf Ranking") in 2012. As a professional, he has been ranked as high as second in the [Official World Golf Ranking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_World_Golf_Ranking "Official World Golf Ranking"), doing so in June 2017.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-beall-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-owgr4-12-21-7)

## Early life and amateur career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hideki_Matsuyama&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and amateur career")]

Matsuyama was born on 25 February 1992 in [Matsuyama, Ehime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matsuyama,_Ehime "Matsuyama, Ehime"), [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"). He was introduced to golf at the age of four by his father. During eighth grade, he transferred to Meitoku Gijuku Junior & Senior High School in [Kochi Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C5%8Dchi_Prefecture "Kōchi Prefecture"), in search of a better golf environment.

Matsuyama studied at [Tohoku Fukushi University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tohoku_Fukushi_University "Tohoku Fukushi University") in [Sendai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai "Sendai"). He won the 2010 [Asian Amateur Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_Amateur_Championship "Asian Amateur Championship") with a score of 68-69-65-67=269.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-8) This gave him the chance to compete as an amateur in the [2011 Masters Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Masters_Tournament "2011 Masters Tournament"), becoming the first Japanese amateur to do so. At the Masters, Matsuyama was the leading amateur and won the Silver Cup, which is presented to the lowest scoring amateur.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-9) He was the only amateur to make the cut.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-10) A week after his victory, he finished in a tie for third at the [Japan Open Golf Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Open_Golf_Championship "Japan Open Golf Championship"), which is an event on the [Japan Golf Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Golf_Tour "Japan Golf Tour").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-11)

In 2011, Matsuyama won the [gold medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf_at_the_2011_Summer_Universiade "Golf at the 2011 Summer Universiade") at the [2011 World University Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Summer_Universiade "2011 Summer Universiade"). He also led the Japan team to the gold medal in the team event. In October 2011, he also successfully defended his title at the Asian Amateur Championship.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-12) In November, Matsuyama won the [Mitsui Sumitomo Visa Taiheiyo Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitsui_Sumitomo_Visa_Taiheiyo_Masters "Mitsui Sumitomo Visa Taiheiyo Masters") on the [Japan Golf Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Golf_Tour "Japan Golf Tour") while still an amateur.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-13)

In August 2012, Matsuyama reached number one in the [World Amateur Golf Ranking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Amateur_Golf_Ranking "World Amateur Golf Ranking").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-14)

## Professional career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hideki_Matsuyama&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Professional career")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/20210430kensyo07.jpg/250px-20210430kensyo07.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20210430kensyo07.jpg)

[Yoshihide Suga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoshihide_Suga "Yoshihide Suga") held a ceremony at [Naikaku Sōri Daijin Kantei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naikaku_S%C5%8Dri_Daijin_Kantei "Naikaku Sōri Daijin Kantei") to honor Matsuyama in 2021.

### Japan Golf Tour

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hideki_Matsuyama&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Japan Golf Tour")]

Matsuyama turned professional in April 2013 and won his second professional tournament, the 2013 [Tsuruya Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsuruya_Open "Tsuruya Open") on the Japan Golf Tour. Five weeks later, Matsuyama won his third title on the Japan Golf Tour at the [Diamond Cup Golf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond_Cup_Golf "Diamond Cup Golf") tournament. Following a top 10 finish at the [2013 U.S. Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_U.S._Open_(golf) "2013 U.S. Open (golf)"), Matsuyama entered the top 50 of the [Official World Golf Ranking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_World_Golf_Ranking "Official World Golf Ranking"). He won his fourth Japan Golf Tour event in September at the [Fujisankei Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujisankei_Classic "Fujisankei Classic"). Matsuyama would win his fifth Japan Golf Tour event in December at the [Casio World Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casio_World_Open "Casio World Open"). The win also made Matsuyama the first rookie to lead the Japan Tour's money list.

### PGA Tour

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hideki_Matsuyama&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: PGA Tour")]

For 2014, Matsuyama qualified for the PGA Tour through non-member earnings. In just seven PGA Tour-sanctioned events, Matsuyama had six top-25 finishes, including a T-6 at the [2013 Open Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Open_Championship "2013 Open Championship").

Matsuyama earned his first PGA Tour win at the [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_PGA_Tour "2014 PGA Tour")[Memorial Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Tournament "Memorial Tournament"), beating [Kevin Na](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Na "Kevin Na") in a playoff and moving to a career-high OWGR ranking of 13th. The win was the first for a Japanese player since [Ryuji Imada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryuji_Imada "Ryuji Imada") in 2008. In his first full season as a PGA tour member, he finished 28th in the FedEx Cup standings.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-15)

Matsuyama would win his sixth Japan Golf Tour event late in the 2014 season. In November, the victory came at the [Dunlop Phoenix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunlop_Phoenix "Dunlop Phoenix") in a playoff over [Hiroshi Iwata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshi_Iwata "Hiroshi Iwata").

Matsuyama finished fifth at the [2015 Masters Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Masters_Tournament "2015 Masters Tournament"), the best major finish of his career to that point.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-16) He finished 16th in the [FedEx Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FedEx_Cup "FedEx Cup") standings. In 8–11 October, he played for the International Team in the [2015 Presidents Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Presidents_Cup "2015 Presidents Cup") and went 2–1–1 (win–loss–half).

On 7 February 2016, Matsuyama won the [Waste Management Phoenix Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waste_Management_Phoenix_Open "Waste Management Phoenix Open") in a playoff with [Rickie Fowler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rickie_Fowler "Rickie Fowler"). He secured his victory on the fourth hole.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-17) The win moved him to 12th in the Official World Golf Ranking, the highest in his career.

On 16 October 2016, Matsuyama captured the [Japan Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Open_Golf_Championship "Japan Open Golf Championship") by three strokes over [Yuta Ikeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuta_Ikeda "Yuta Ikeda") and [Lee Kyoung-hoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Kyoung-hoon "Lee Kyoung-hoon"). The win was Matsuyama's first title at his country's national open and his seventh victory in Japan. The title gives Matsuyama victories in four of the [Japan Golf Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Golf_Tour "Japan Golf Tour")'s five ¥200,000,000 events.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-18)

On 30 October 2016, Matsuyama followed up his Japan Open triumph by winning the [WGC-HSBC Champions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WGC-HSBC_Champions "WGC-HSBC Champions"), colloquially known as "Asia's Major", in [Shanghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai "Shanghai"). Matsuyama became the first Asian golfer to claim a [World Golf Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Golf_Championship "World Golf Championship") since the series was inaugurated in 1999. With the victory, Matsuyama rose to number 6 in the Official World Golf Ranking, his highest position and the second highest ever by a Japanese player after [Masashi Ozaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masashi_Ozaki "Masashi Ozaki"), who achieved a ranking of fifth.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-tm-19) He later moved up to fifth in the world after the [Farmers Insurance Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farmers_Insurance_Open "Farmers Insurance Open"). On 13 November 2016, Matsuyama won his second [Taiheiyo Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiheiyo_Masters "Taiheiyo Masters"), following his victory as a 19-year-old amateur in 2011. He romped to a seven-shot win over South Korea's [Song Young-han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_Young-han "Song Young-han").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-tm-19) On 4 December 2016, Matsuyama won the [Hero World Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_World_Challenge "Hero World Challenge") in the Bahamas.

Although he was the highest ranked male Japanese golfer at the time, Matsuyama withdrew from participating in the [2016 Rio Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics") out of concern about the [2016 Zika virus epidemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015%E2%80%932016_Zika_virus_epidemic "2015–2016 Zika virus epidemic"), which caused several of the world's top players to withdraw from the Olympic golf event.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-2016olympics-20)

In Matsuyama's return to the [Waste Management Phoenix Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waste_Management_Phoenix_Open "Waste Management Phoenix Open"), he again entered a playoff on Sunday to defend his title, this time against [Webb Simpson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webb_Simpson "Webb Simpson"). On the fourth playoff hole, Matsuyama made birdie to win the tournament for the second time in as many years. After finishing second in the [2017 U.S. Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_U.S._Open_(golf) "2017 U.S. Open (golf)") at Erin Hills, while the top three players in the world at the time ([Dustin Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dustin_Johnson "Dustin Johnson"), [Rory McIlroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rory_McIlroy "Rory McIlroy") and [Jason Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Day "Jason Day")) failed to make the cut, Matsuyama reached 2nd in the [Official World Golf Ranking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_World_Golf_Ranking "Official World Golf Ranking"), his highest ever, and the highest ever for a male Japanese golfer.

The 2017 season has been a breakthrough year with Matsuyama winning three Tour titles, including his first [World Golf Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_WGC-HSBC_Champions#Final_round "2016 WGC-HSBC Champions"), and three second-place finishes in his first 15 events, as well as winning $5,945,990, putting him second on the money list behind [Dustin Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dustin_Johnson "Dustin Johnson"), before the month of July. He then won the [WGC-Bridgestone Invitational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_WGC-Bridgestone_Invitational "2017 WGC-Bridgestone Invitational") in August, shooting a course record-tying 61 in the final round to win by five strokes.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-21)

At the 2017 PGA Championship, Matsuyama had opening rounds of 70–64 to share the 36-hold lead, with [Kevin Kisner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Kisner "Kevin Kisner") at Quail Hollow.

In December 2019, Matsuyama played on the International team at the [2019 Presidents Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Presidents_Cup "2019 Presidents Cup") at [Royal Melbourne Golf Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Melbourne_Golf_Club "Royal Melbourne Golf Club") in Australia. The U.S. team won, 16–14. Matsuyama went 2–1–1 and halved his Sunday singles match against [Tony Finau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Finau "Tony Finau").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-22)

On 11 April 2021, Matsuyama won the [Masters Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Masters_Tournament "2021 Masters Tournament"), becoming both the first Japanese player and the first Asian-born player to win the tournament. He finished with an overall score of 278 (−10), one shot ahead of runner-up [Will Zalatoris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Zalatoris "Will Zalatoris").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-23) At the conclusion of the tournament, Matsuyama's caddie, Shota Hayafuji, bowed to the 18th fairway of the [Augusta course](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusta_National_Golf_Club "Augusta National Golf Club") as a gesture of Japanese respect.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-24)

In August, Matsuyama finished in a tie for 3rd place at the [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_individual "Golf at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Men's individual"). He lost in a 7-man playoff for the bronze medal.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-25) The following week Matsuyama was tied for the lead after 72 holes at the [WGC-FedEx St. Jude Invitational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_WGC-FedEx_St._Jude_Invitational "2021 WGC-FedEx St. Jude Invitational"). He was beaten in the playoff when [Abraham Ancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Ancer "Abraham Ancer") birdied the second extra hole.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-26)

In October 2021, Matsuyama won the [Zozo Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zozo_Championship "Zozo Championship") at [Narashino Country Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narashino_Country_Club "Narashino Country Club"). The Zozo Championship is the only PGA Tour event held in Japan. Matsuyama won by five strokes over [Cameron Tringale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron_Tringale "Cameron Tringale") and [Brendan Steele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brendan_Steele "Brendan Steele").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-27)

On 16 January 2022, Matsuyama won the [Sony Open in Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Open_in_Hawaii "Sony Open in Hawaii"); having made up a five-shot deficit on the back nine to get into a [playoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playoff_(golf) "Playoff (golf)") with [Russell Henley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Henley "Russell Henley"), he made an [eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eagle_(golf) "Eagle (golf)") on the first extra hole to claim the victory. It was his eighth win on the PGA Tour, tying [K. J. Choi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K._J._Choi "K. J. Choi") for most tour victories by an Asian-born player.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-28)

On 2 June 2022, at the [Memorial Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Tournament "Memorial Tournament") at Muirfield Village Golf Club in Dublin, Ohio, Matsuyama was disqualified midway through his first round due to having a white paint-like substance on the face of his 3-wood. The substance was said to have been applied by his equipment technician to help with alignment.

Matsuyama qualified for the International team at the [2022 Presidents Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Presidents_Cup "2022 Presidents Cup"); he won one, tied one and lost three of the five matches he played.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-29)

On 18 February 2024, Matsuyama won the [Genesis Invitational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_Invitational "Genesis Invitational"). He entered the final round six strokes off the lead, but overcame the deficit, shooting a 62 to win his first PGA Tour event since the 2022 [Sony Open in Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Open_in_Hawaii "Sony Open in Hawaii").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-genesis-6) Matsuyama posted the second-lowest round in course history. It was also the lowest in the fourth round of a tournament at [Riviera Country Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riviera_Country_Club "Riviera Country Club").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-30)

In August, Matsuyama won the bronze medal at the [2024 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_individual "Golf at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Men's individual"). He finished two shots behind [Scottie Scheffler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottie_Scheffler "Scottie Scheffler"), the gold medalist, and one shot behind [Tommy Fleetwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Fleetwood "Tommy Fleetwood"), the silver medalist, with a score of 267 (−17).[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-31) Later that month, he won the [FedEx St. Jude Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FedEx_St._Jude_Championship "FedEx St. Jude Championship") by two strokes with a score of 263 (−17). Matsuyama nearly lost control of a five shot lead in the final round after errant shots on the back nine, but birdies on the last two holes brought him his 10th victory on the PGA Tour.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-32)

In January, Matsuyama won [The Sentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sentry_(Hawaii) "The Sentry (Hawaii)"), three strokes ahead of [Collin Morikawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Morikawa "Collin Morikawa"). His winning score of 35-under 257 broke the PGA Tour scoring record in relation to par, previously set by [Cameron Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron_Smith_(golfer) "Cameron Smith (golfer)") in 2022 at 34-under total, also at The Sentry.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-33)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hideki_Matsuyama&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Matsuyama and his wife Mei (married in January 2017) have a daughter born in July 2017.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-35)

After winning a bronze medal at the Paris Olympics in August 2024, Matsuyama became the victim of a robbery in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), while in the city during a layover to [Memphis, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee") for the [FedEx St. Jude Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FedEx_St._Jude_Championship "FedEx St. Jude Championship"). His wallet was stolen, and both his caddie and his coach had their passports stolen. Matsuyama's Olympic medal was not among the stolen items.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama#cite_note-36)

**Yuta Sugiura** (杉浦 悠太, _Sugiura Yuta_; born 12 September 2001) is a Japanese [professional golfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_golfer "Professional golfer") who plays on the [Korn Ferry Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korn_Ferry_Tour "Korn Ferry Tour"), where he claimed his first win at the 2026 [AdventHealth Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AdventHealth_Championship "AdventHealth Championship"). He also plays on the [Japan Golf Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Golf_Tour "Japan Golf Tour") where he has three victories and was the [2025 Rookie of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Golf_Tour_Rookie_of_the_Year "Japan Golf Tour Rookie of the Year").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuta_Sugiura#cite_note-1)

## Amateur career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yuta_Sugiura&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Amateur career")]

Sugiura was born in [Takahama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takahama,_Aichi "Takahama, Aichi"), Aichi Prefecture. He graduated from Fukui Institute of Technology High School, before attending [Nihon University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nihon_University "Nihon University") from 2020 to 2023.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuta_Sugiura#cite_note-JGTOBio-2)

In 2018, Sugiura won the Japan Junior Championship. He finished 4th at the 2020 [Australian Master of the Amateurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Master_of_the_Amateurs "Australian Master of the Amateurs"), six strokes behind winner [Sahith Theegala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahith_Theegala "Sahith Theegala").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuta_Sugiura#cite_note-3)

He played an active role on the national team, and won the 2022 [Nomura Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomura_Cup "Nomura Cup") in the Philippines, both with the team and individually. His team finished 4th at the [2022 Asian Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf_at_the_2022_Asian_Games_%E2%80%93_Men's_team "Golf at the 2022 Asian Games – Men's team").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuta_Sugiura#cite_note-JGTOBio-2)

Sugiura tied for 3rd at the 2022 [Japan Open Golf Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Open_Golf_Championship "Japan Open Golf Championship"). In 2023, his final year at university, he won the [Japan Challenge Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Challenge_Tour "Japan Challenge Tour")'s Dunlop Phoenix Challenge, which earned him a spot in the 50th [Dunlop Phoenix Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunlop_Phoenix_Tournament "Dunlop Phoenix Tournament"), where he became the seventh amateur to win on the [Japan Golf Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Golf_Tour "Japan Golf Tour"), winning by three strokes after starting the day a stroke behind overnight leader [Hideki Matsuyama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama "Hideki Matsuyama").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuta_Sugiura#cite_note-4)

## Professional career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yuta_Sugiura&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Professional career")]

Sugiura turned professional the day after he won the [Dunlop Phoenix Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunlop_Phoenix_Tournament "Dunlop Phoenix Tournament") in November 2023 and joined the [Japan Golf Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Golf_Tour "Japan Golf Tour"). In 2024, he won the [Japan PGA Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_PGA_Championship "Japan PGA Championship") in his first appearance. He finished top- 10 in five consecutive tournaments including a runner-up at the [Kansai Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansai_Open "Kansai Open"), to finish 11th in the season rankings.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuta_Sugiura#cite_note-JGTOBio-2)

In 2025, Sugiura was runner-up at the [Fujisankei Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujisankei_Classic "Fujisankei Classic") and the [International Series Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Series_Japan "International Series Japan"), behind [Lucas Herbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_Herbert "Lucas Herbert"). He qualified for his first major, the [2025 U.S. Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_U.S._Open_(golf) "2025 U.S. Open (golf)"), in the qualifier at Tarao Country Club, alongside [Jinichiro Kozuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jinichiro_Kozuma "Jinichiro Kozuma") and [Scott Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Vincent "Scott Vincent"). He won the [ACN Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACN_Championship "ACN Championship") and was named [Japan Golf Tour Rookie of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Golf_Tour_Rookie_of_the_Year "Japan Golf Tour Rookie of the Year").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuta_Sugiura#cite_note-5)

Sugiura joined the 2026 [Korn Ferry Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korn_Ferry_Tour "Korn Ferry Tour"), where he won the [AdventHealth Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AdventHealth_Championship "AdventHealth Championship") in [Kansas City, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri "Kansas City, Missouri").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuta_Sugiura#cite_note-6)

**Matsuyama** (松山市, _Matsuyama-shi_; Japanese:[[matsɯꜜjama]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Japanese "Help:IPA/Japanese")) is the capital [city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities_of_Japan "Cities of Japan") of [Ehime Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ehime_Prefecture "Ehime Prefecture"), on the island of [Shikoku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shikoku "Shikoku"), in Japan and is also Shikoku's largest city. As of 1 October 2022[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Matsuyama&action=edit), the city had an estimated population of 494,100 in 243,541 households and a [population density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_density "Population density") of 1,200 persons per km 2.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matsuyama,_Ehime#cite_note-Matsuyama-hp-1) The total area of the city is 429.35 square kilometres (165.77 sq mi).

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Matsuyama&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Geography")]

Matsuyama is located in central Ehime Prefecture, facing the [Seto Inland Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seto_Inland_Sea "Seto Inland Sea") to the north, the mountains of the Takanawa Peninsula to the north and east, and the Saragamine Mountain Range, an extension of the [Shikoku Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shikoku_Mountains "Shikoku Mountains"), to the south. It is located on the northeastern portion of the Dōgo Plain. The city also includes the Kutsuna Islands, an archipelago of 29 islands in the Seto Inland Sea.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Matsuyama&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: History")]

The area of Matsuyama was part of ancient [Iyo Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iyo_Province "Iyo Province"). [Dōgo Onsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C5%8Dgo_Onsen "Dōgo Onsen") was already famous in the [Asuka period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asuka_period "Asuka period"), and [Shōtoku Taishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sh%C5%8Dtoku_Taishi "Shōtoku Taishi") visited the spa in the year 596. It is also mentioned in passing in _[The Tale of Genji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Tale\_of\_Genji "The Tale of Genji")_. At the end of the [Heian period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heian_period "Heian period"), Kōno Michinobu supported [Minamoto no Yoritomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minamoto_no_Yoritomo "Minamoto no Yoritomo") against the [Heike clan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heike_clan "Heike clan") during the [Genpei War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genpei_War "Genpei War") and was awarded with a position as _[shugo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shugo "Shugo")_ of Iyo Province. In the [Muromachi period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muromachi_period "Muromachi period"), the clan made their stronghold at [Yuzuki Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuzuki_Castle "Yuzuki Castle"), near Dōgo Onsen, and developed the port of [Mitsuhama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitsuhama "Mitsuhama") to the west to link the area to [Honshū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honsh%C5%AB "Honshū") and [Kyūshū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ky%C5%ABsh%C5%AB "Kyūshū"). The clan was conquered by [Toyotomi Hideyoshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyotomi_Hideyoshi "Toyotomi Hideyoshi") during his invasion of Shikoku, and later the area became part of [Iyo-Matsuyama Domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iyo-Matsuyama_Domain "Iyo-Matsuyama Domain") under the [Tokugawa shogunate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokugawa_shogunate "Tokugawa shogunate"). A _[jōkamachi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C5%8Dkamachi "Jōkamachi")_ developed around [Matsuyama Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matsuyama_Castle_(Iyo) "Matsuyama Castle (Iyo)"), and this is the core of the modern city. The city was established with the creation of the modern municipality system on December 15, 1889. The city was bombed on July 26, 1945, in the final stages of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), with 251 civilians killed and over 55% of the city area destroyed.

In the twentieth century, various [mergers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onsen_District,_Ehime "Onsen District, Ehime") joined Matsuyama with neighboring towns of [Dōgo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C5%8Dgo_Onsen "Dōgo Onsen"), [Mitsuhama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitsuhama "Mitsuhama"), and other townships, aided by [urban sprawl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_sprawl "Urban sprawl"), creating a seamless modern city that now ranks as the largest in Shikoku. On October 1, 2018, Matsuyama absorbed the city of [Hōjō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C5%8Dj%C5%8D,_Ehime "Hōjō, Ehime"), and town of [Nakajima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakajima,_Ehime "Nakajima, Ehime") (from the former [Onsen District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onsen_District,_Ehime "Onsen District, Ehime")).

## Government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Matsuyama&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Government")]

Matsuyama has a [mayor-council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor-council "Mayor-council") form of government with a directly elected mayor and a [unicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unicameral "Unicameral") city council of 42 members. Matsuyama, together with Kumakōgen, contributes 16 members to the Ehime Prefectural Assembly. In terms of national politics, the city is split between Ehime 1st district and Ehime 2nd district of the [lower house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Representatives_of_Japan "House of Representatives of Japan") of the [Diet of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diet_of_Japan "Diet of Japan").

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Matsuyama&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Economy")]

Matsuyama is a major regional commercial center. Key industries include agriculture represented by [mandarin oranges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandarin_orange "Mandarin orange"), tourism centered around Dōgo Onsen and Matsuyama Castle, and manufacturing centered on chemical fibers. Industrial areas spread along the coast near airports and harbors, including the Teijin Group's largest production base, and factories of Miura ([boiler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boiler "Boiler") manufacturer), [Iseki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iseki "Iseki") ([tractor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tractor "Tractor") and engine equipment),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matsuyama,_Ehime#cite_note-5) Hatada Ichiroku (Japanese style [confectionery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confectionery "Confectionery")), Poem, a food processing division of Pom (Ehime Drink Company), and the [retailing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retailer "Retailer") companies Fuji and Daiki all have their headquarters in Matsuyama.

### Primary and secondary education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Matsuyama&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Primary and secondary education")]

Matsuyama has 62 public elementary schools and 31 public middle schools operated by the city government. The city has seven public high schools operated by the Ehime Prefectural Board of Education, including the [Ehime Prefectural Matsuyama Central Senior High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ehime_Prefectural_Matsuyama_Central_Senior_High_School "Ehime Prefectural Matsuyama Central Senior High School") and the [Ehime Prefectural Matsuyama Higashi High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ehime_Prefectural_Matsuyama_Higashi_High_School "Ehime Prefectural Matsuyama Higashi High School") and two national high schools operated by Ehime University. There are two private combined middle/high schools and 11 private high schools. The prefecture also operates two special education schools for the handicapped.

## Local attractions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Matsuyama&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Local attractions")]

[![Image 32](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/Dogo_Hot_Spring5%28Matsuyama_City%29.JPG/250px-Dogo_Hot_Spring5%28Matsuyama_City%29.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dogo_Hot_Spring5(Matsuyama_City).JPG)

Dōgo Onsen Honkan

[![Image 33](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/Dogo-station2004-7-3.jpg/250px-Dogo-station2004-7-3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dogo-station2004-7-3.jpg)

Botchan Ressha at Dogo Station, Matsuyama

The city is known for its [hot springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_springs "Hot springs") ([onsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onsen "Onsen")), among the oldest in Japan, and is home to the [Dōgo Onsen Honkan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C5%8Dgo_Onsen "Dōgo Onsen"), a Meiji Period wooden public bathhouse dating from 1894.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matsuyama,_Ehime#cite_note-7) A second favorite tourist spot is [Matsuyama Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matsuyama_Castle_(Iyo) "Matsuyama Castle (Iyo)"). Eight of the eighty-eight temples in the [Shikoku Pilgrimage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shikoku_Pilgrimage "Shikoku Pilgrimage") are in Matsuyama.

Buddhist temples in Matsuyama include [Ishite-ji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishite-ji "Ishite-ji") (石手寺), [Taisan-ji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taisan-ji_(Matsuyama) "Taisan-ji (Matsuyama)") (太山寺), and [Jōdo-ji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C5%8Ddo-ji_(Matsuyama) "Jōdo-ji (Matsuyama)") (浄土寺), all dating back to the 8th century, although the oldest surviving buildings are from the early 14th century, as well as [Hōgon-ji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C5%8Dgon-ji_(Matsuyama) "Hōgon-ji (Matsuyama)") (宝厳寺), [Taihō-ji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taih%C5%8D-ji_(Matsuyama) "Taihō-ji (Matsuyama)") (大宝寺) and [Enmyō-ji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enmy%C5%8D-ji_(Matsuyama) "Enmyō-ji (Matsuyama)") (円明寺). Shrines of the city include [Isaniwa Jinja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaniwa_Jinja "Isaniwa Jinja") (伊佐爾波神社), built in 1667.

The [haiku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haiku "Haiku") poet [Masaoka Shiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masaoka_Shiki "Masaoka Shiki") lived in Matsuyama. His house, now known as the [Shiki-do](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiki-do?action=edit&redlink=1 "Shiki-do (page does not exist)"), and a museum, the [Shiki Memorial Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiki_Memorial_Museum "Shiki Memorial Museum"), are popular attractions, and the centerpieces of the city's claim as a center of the international haiku movement. Other haiku poets associated with Matsuyama include [Kurita Chodō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurita_Chod%C5%8D "Kurita Chodō"), whose [Kōshin-an](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C5%8Dshin-an "Kōshin-an") was visited by [Kobayashi Issa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobayashi_Issa "Kobayashi Issa"), Shiki's followers, [Takahama Kyoshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takahama_Kyoshi "Takahama Kyoshi") and [Kawahigashi Hekigoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kawahigashi_Hekigoto "Kawahigashi Hekigoto"), and [Taneda Santōka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taneda_Sant%C5%8Dka "Taneda Santōka"). Santoka's house, known as Isso-an, is also a tourist attraction and is periodically open to the public. The Matsuyama Declaration of 1999 proposed the formation of the International Haiku Research Center, and the first [Masaoka Shiki International Haiku Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masaoka_Shiki_International_Haiku_Awards "Masaoka Shiki International Haiku Awards") were given in 2000. Recipients have included [Yves Bonnefoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yves_Bonnefoy "Yves Bonnefoy") (2000), [Cor van den Heuvel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cor_van_den_Heuvel "Cor van den Heuvel") (2002) and [Gary Snyder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Snyder "Gary Snyder") (2004).

The famed novel _[Botchan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botchan "Botchan")_ by [Natsume Sōseki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natsume_S%C5%8Dseki "Natsume Sōseki") is set in Matsuyama. As a result, there are numerous sites and locales named after the main character, including [Botchan Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botchan_Stadium "Botchan Stadium"), the [Botchan Ressha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botchan_Ressha "Botchan Ressha") (an antique train that runs on the city's tramway), and Botchan [dango](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dango "Dango").

Matsuyama also figures in several works by [Shiba Ryōtarō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiba_Ry%C5%8Dtar%C5%8D "Shiba Ryōtarō"), notably his popular novel, _[Saka no Ue no Kumo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saka\_no\_Ue\_no\_Kumo "Saka no Ue no Kumo")_ [Clouds Above the Hill] (1969). In anticipation of the upcoming [NHK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NHK "NHK")[Taiga drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiga_drama "Taiga drama")[adaptation of _Saka no Ue no Kumo_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saka_no_Ue_no_Kumo_(TV_series) "Saka no Ue no Kumo (TV series)"), a [Saka no Ue no Kumo Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saka_no_Ue_no_Kumo_Museum "Saka no Ue no Kumo Museum") was established in 2007.

Matsuyama was also the setting of a 1907 novel about the [Russo-Japanese War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Japanese_War "Russo-Japanese War"), _As the Hague Ordains_, by American writer [Eliza Ruhamah Scidmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliza_Ruhamah_Scidmore "Eliza Ruhamah Scidmore"). Matsuyama figures in the novel because the city housed a camp for Russian prisoners during the war. A Russian cemetery commemorates this important episode in Matsuyama history. The [Russo-Japanese War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Japanese_War "Russo-Japanese War") is also remembered in Matsuyama because of the contributions of two Japanese military leaders, the Akiyama brothers, [Akiyama Saneyuki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akiyama_Saneyuki "Akiyama Saneyuki") and [Akiyama Yoshifuru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akiyama_Yoshifuru "Akiyama Yoshifuru"), who were born in the city.

Matsuyama has several important museums. [The Museum of Art, Ehime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Museum_of_Art,_Ehime "The Museum of Art, Ehime") is the city's main art museum, its collections emphasizing the works of regional artists. The [Shiki Memorial Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiki_Memorial_Museum "Shiki Memorial Museum") is a museum that focuses on the life and work of [Masaoka Shiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masaoka_Shiki "Masaoka Shiki"), with special attention to his contribution to [haiku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haiku "Haiku"). The [Saka no Ue no Kumo Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saka_no_Ue_no_Kumo_Museum "Saka no Ue no Kumo Museum") features exhibits connected with the novel and television series. There is a [Juzo Itami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juzo_Itami "Juzo Itami") museum dedicated to the film director.

Products ([meibutsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meibutsu "Meibutsu")) of Matsuyama include [tarts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tart "Tart") and Botchan [dango](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dango "Dango"). In the 17th century, the lord of Matsuyama castle Sadayuki Matsudaira (松平定行) introduced the process of tart-making, originally brought to Japan by the Portuguese, to Matsuyama. At first it was a [Castella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castella "Castella") with jam. According to legend Sadayuki made some changes, such as adding [red bean paste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_bean_paste "Red bean paste"). Now there are many kinds and makers of tarts in Matsuyama; some add [yuzu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuzu "Yuzu") paste or [chestnut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chestnut "Chestnut") to the red bean paste. In addition to tarts, [Botchan dango](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botchan_dango?action=edit&redlink=1 "Botchan dango (page does not exist)") is also a product of Matsuyama. Botchan dango was named after the novel _[Botchan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botchan "Botchan")_ by [Natsume Sōseki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natsume_S%C5%8Dseki "Natsume Sōseki"). It consists of three bean paste beads of three flavors, [matcha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matcha "Matcha"), egg, and red bean paste. Within the paste is contained [mochi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mochi "Mochi").

Matsuyama is the site of a number of festivals, including the Dogo Festival, held in the spring, the Matsuyama Festival, held in August, and the Fall Festival, held in October, which features battling [mikoshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikoshi "Mikoshi").

The [Ehime Mandarin Pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ehime_Mandarin_Pirates "Ehime Mandarin Pirates") also represent the city in the [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball")[Shikoku Island League Plus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shikoku_Island_League_Plus "Shikoku Island League Plus").

**Takahama** (高浜市, _Takahama-shi_) is a [city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities_of_Japan "Cities of Japan") located in central [Aichi Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aichi_Prefecture "Aichi Prefecture"), Japan. As of 1 October 2019[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Takahama,_Aichi&action=edit), the city had an estimated population of 48,736 in 20,500 households,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takahama,_Aichi#cite_note-1) and a [population density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_density "Population density") of 3,717 persons per km 2. The total area of the city is 13.11 square kilometres (5.06 sq mi).

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Takahama,_Aichi&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/View_of_Takahama_City_from_Ooyama_Park.jpg/250px-View_of_Takahama_City_from_Ooyama_Park.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:View_of_Takahama_City_from_Ooyama_Park.jpg)

[Skyline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skyline "Skyline") of Tahara City from Ooyama Park

Takahama is situated in south-central Aichi Prefecture, on Kinuura Bay at the head of [Atsumi Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atsumi_Peninsula "Atsumi Peninsula").

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Takahama,_Aichi&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Climate")]

The city has a climate characterized by hot and humid summers, and relatively mild winters ([Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification")_Cfa_). The average annual temperature in Takahama is 15.7°C. The average annual rainfall is 1592 mm with September as the wettest month. The temperatures are highest on average in August, at around 27.8°C, and lowest in January, at around 4.4°C.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takahama,_Aichi#cite_note-2)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Takahama,_Aichi&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: History")]

### Late modern period

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Takahama,_Aichi&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Late modern period")]

Takahama Village was created within [Hekikai District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hekikai_District,_Aichi "Hekikai District, Aichi") on October 1, 1889. It was raised to town status on July 9, 1900, and annexed neighboring Yoshihama and Takatori villages on May 1, 1906.

### Contemporary history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Takahama,_Aichi&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Contemporary history")]

In 1956, Kinuura bridge, connecting Takahama and [Handa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handa,_Aichi "Handa, Aichi") was opened.

Takahama was raised to city status on December 1, 1970, causing Hekikai District to cease to exist, along with Higashi-Kasugai District which ceased to exist following the elevation of [Owariasahi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owariasahi "Owariasahi") to city status at the same date.

## Government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Takahama,_Aichi&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Government")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Takahama_City_Hall_in_Nov._2018_ac.jpg/250px-Takahama_City_Hall_in_Nov._2018_ac.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Takahama_City_Hall_in_Nov._2018_ac.jpg)

Takahama City Hall

Takahama has a [mayor-council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor-council "Mayor-council") form of government with a directly elected mayor and a [unicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unicameral "Unicameral") city legislature of 16 members. The city contributes one member to the Aichi Prefectural Assembly. In terms of national politics, the city is part of Aichi District 13 of the [lower house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Representatives_of_Japan "House of Representatives of Japan") of the [Diet of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diet_of_Japan "Diet of Japan").

**Aichi Prefecture** (愛知県, _Aichi-ken_; Japanese pronunciation:[[aꜜi.tɕi,ai.tɕi̥ꜜ.keɴ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Japanese "Help:IPA/Japanese")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aichi_Prefecture#cite_note-2)) is a [prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefectures_of_Japan "Prefectures of Japan") of [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") located in the [Chūbu region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C5%ABbu_region "Chūbu region") of [Honshū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honsh%C5%AB "Honshū").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aichi_Prefecture#cite_note-Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_2002-3):11,126 Aichi Prefecture has a population of 7,461,111 (as of 1 January 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aichi_Prefecture&action=edit)) and a geographic area of 5,172.92 [square kilometres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_kilometre "Square kilometre") (1,997.28[sq mi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_mile "Square mile")) with a population density of 1,442 inhabitants per square kilometre (3,730/sq mi). Aichi Prefecture borders [Mie Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mie_Prefecture "Mie Prefecture") to the west, [Gifu Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gifu_Prefecture "Gifu Prefecture") and [Nagano Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagano_Prefecture "Nagano Prefecture") to the north, and [Shizuoka Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shizuoka_Prefecture "Shizuoka Prefecture") to the east. [Nagoya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagoya "Nagoya") is the capital and largest city of the prefecture.

## Overview

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aichi_Prefecture&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Overview")]

[Nagoya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagoya "Nagoya") is the capital and largest city of Aichi Prefecture, and the [fourth-largest city in Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Largest_cities_in_Japan_by_population_by_decade "Largest cities in Japan by population by decade"). Other major cities include [Toyota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota,_Aichi "Toyota, Aichi"), [Okazaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okazaki,_Aichi "Okazaki, Aichi"), and [Ichinomiya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ichinomiya,_Aichi "Ichinomiya, Aichi"). Aichi Prefecture and Nagoya form the core of the [Chūkyō metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C5%ABky%C5%8D_metropolitan_area "Chūkyō metropolitan area"), the [third-largest metropolitan area in Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_metropolitan_areas_in_Japan "List of metropolitan areas in Japan") and one of the largest [metropolitan areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area "Metropolitan area") in the world.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aichi_Prefecture#cite_note-Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_2002-3):685 Aichi Prefecture is located on Japan's [Pacific Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") coast and forms part of the [Tōkai region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Dkai_region "Tōkai region"), a [subregion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subregion "Subregion") of the Chūbu region and [Kansai region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansai_region "Kansai region"). Aichi Prefecture is home to the [Toyota Motor Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota "Toyota"). Aichi Prefecture had many locations with the [Higashiyama Zoo and Botanical Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higashiyama_Zoo_and_Botanical_Gardens "Higashiyama Zoo and Botanical Gardens"), the [Chubu Centrair International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chubu_Centrair_International_Airport "Chubu Centrair International Airport"), and the [Legoland Japan Resort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legoland_Japan_Resort "Legoland Japan Resort").

Satellite photo of Mikawa Bay

Located near the centre of the Japanese main island of [Honshu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honshu "Honshu"), Aichi Prefecture faces the [Ise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ise_Bay "Ise Bay") and [Mikawa Bays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikawa_Bay "Mikawa Bay") to the south and borders [Shizuoka Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shizuoka_Prefecture "Shizuoka Prefecture") to the east, [Nagano Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagano_Prefecture "Nagano Prefecture") to the northeast, [Gifu Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gifu_Prefecture "Gifu Prefecture") to the north, and [Mie Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mie_Prefecture "Mie Prefecture") to the west. It measures 106 km (66 mi) east to west and 94 km (58 mi) south to north and forms a major portion of the [Nōbi Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C5%8Dbi_Plain "Nōbi Plain"). With an area of 5,172.48 square kilometres (1,997.11 sq mi) it accounts for approximately 1.36% of the total surface area of Japan. The highest spot is [Chausuyama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chausuyama_(Aichi) "Chausuyama (Aichi)") at 1,415 m (4,642 ft) above sea level.

The western part of the prefecture is dominated by [Nagoya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagoya,_Aichi "Nagoya, Aichi"), Japan's third largest city, and its suburbs, while the eastern part is less densely populated but still contains several major industrial centres. Due to its robust economy, for the period from October 2005 to October 2006, Aichi was the fastest growing prefecture in terms of population, beating [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo"), at 7.4% and around with after [Saitama Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saitama_Prefecture "Saitama Prefecture").

As of 1 April 2012,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aichi_Prefecture&action=edit) 23% of the total land area of the prefecture was designated as [Natural Parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_parks_of_Japan#History "List of national parks of Japan"), namely the [Aichi Kōgen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aichi_K%C5%8Dgen_Quasi-National_Park "Aichi Kōgen Quasi-National Park"), [Hida-Kisogawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hida-Kisogawa_Quasi-National_Park "Hida-Kisogawa Quasi-National Park"), [Mikawa Wan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikawa_Wan_Quasi-National_Park "Mikawa Wan Quasi-National Park"), and [Tenryū-Okumikawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenry%C5%AB-Okumikawa_Quasi-National_Park "Tenryū-Okumikawa Quasi-National Park") Quasi-National Parks along with seven Prefectural Natural Parks.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aichi_Prefecture#cite_note-NationalPark-4)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aichi_Prefecture&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: History")]

See also: [Historic Sites of Aichi Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historic_Sites_of_Aichi_Prefecture "Historic Sites of Aichi Prefecture")

Originally, the region was divided into two provinces of [Owari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owari_Province "Owari Province") and [Mikawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikawa_Province "Mikawa Province").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aichi_Prefecture#cite_note-Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_2002-3):780 After the [Meiji Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiji_Restoration "Meiji Restoration"), Owari and Mikawa were united into a single entity. In 1871, after the [abolition of the han system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolition_of_the_han_system "Abolition of the han system"), Owari, with the exception of the [Chita Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chita_Peninsula "Chita Peninsula"), was established as Nagoya Prefecture, while Mikawa combined with the Chita Peninsula and formed [Nukata Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nukata_Prefecture "Nukata Prefecture"). Nagoya Prefecture was renamed to Aichi Prefecture in April 1872 and was united with Nukata Prefecture on 27 November of the same year.

The government of Aichi Prefecture is located in the [Aichi Prefectural Government Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aichi_Prefectural_Government_Office "Aichi Prefectural Government Office") in Nagoya, which is the old capital of Owari. The [Aichi Prefectural Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aichi_Prefectural_Police "Aichi Prefectural Police") and its predecessor organisations have been responsible for law enforcement in the prefecture since 1871.

The [Expo 2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expo_2005 "Expo 2005")[World Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_fair "World's fair") was held in [Seto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seto,_Aichi "Seto, Aichi") and [Nagakute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagakute,_Aichi "Nagakute, Aichi").

### Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Aichi_Prefecture&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Etymology")]

In the third volume of the _[Man'yōshū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man'y%C5%8Dsh%C5%AB "Man'yōshū")_ there is a poem by Takechi Kurohito that reads: "The cry of the crane, calling to Sakurada; it sounds like the tide, draining from Ayuchi flats, hearing the crane cry". Ayuchi is the original form of the name _Aichi_, and the [Fujimae tidal flat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujimae-higata "Fujimae-higata") is all that remains of the earlier Ayuchi-gata. It is now a protected area.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aichi_Prefecture#cite_note-pref.aichi.jp-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aichi_Prefecture#cite_note-Kato_2000-7)

For a time, an Aichi Station existed on the [Kansai Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansai_Line "Kansai Line") (at the time the Kansai Railway) between [Nagoya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagoya_Station "Nagoya Station") and [Hatta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatta_Station "Hatta Station") stations, but its role was overtaken by [Sasashima-raibu Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasashima-raibu_Station "Sasashima-raibu Station") on the [Aonami Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aonami_Line "Aonami Line") and [Komeno Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komeno_Station "Komeno Station") on the [Kintetsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kintetsu_Railway "Kintetsu Railway")[Nagoya Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagoya_Line_(Kintetsu) "Nagoya Line (Kintetsu)").

**Sendai** (仙台市, _Sendai-shi_; [[seꜜn.dai,sen.daꜜi.ɕi]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Japanese "Help:IPA/Japanese")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/5/5f/TomJ-Sendai.ogg/TomJ-Sendai.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TomJ-Sendai.ogg "File:TomJ-Sendai.ogg")) is the capital [city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities_of_Japan "Cities of Japan") of [Miyagi Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miyagi_Prefecture "Miyagi Prefecture") and the largest city in the [Tōhoku region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Dhoku_region "Tōhoku region"). As of 1 August 2023[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sendai&action=edit), the city had a population of 1,098,335 in 539,698 households,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai#cite_note-City_of_Sendai_Estimated_Population_and_Demographics-1) making it the [twelfth most populated city in Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Japan "List of cities in Japan").

The modern city was founded in 1600 by the _[daimyō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daimy%C5%8D "Daimyō")_[Date Masamune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Date_Masamune "Date Masamune"). It is nicknamed the _City of Trees_ (杜の都, _Mori no Miyako_); there are [Japanese zelkova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_zelkova "Japanese zelkova") trees lining many of the main thoroughfares such as Jōzenji Street (定禅寺通, _Jōzenji dōri_) and Aoba Street (青葉通, _Aoba dōri_). In the summer, the [Sendai Tanabata Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai_Tanabata_Festival "Sendai Tanabata Festival"), the largest [Tanabata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanabata "Tanabata") festival in Japan, is held. In winter, the trees are decorated with thousands of lights for the Pageant of Starlight (光のページェント, _Hikari no pējento_), lasting through most of December. The city is also home to [Tohoku University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tohoku_University "Tohoku University"), one of the former [Imperial Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Universities "Imperial Universities"). On 11 March 2011, coastal areas of the city suffered catastrophic damage from a [magnitude 9.0 offshore earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_T%C5%8Dhoku_earthquake_and_tsunami "2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai#cite_note-USGS-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai#cite_note-UKFO-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai#cite_note-TELG-4) which triggered a destructive [tsunami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami "Tsunami").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai#cite_note-5)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sendai&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Edo period

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sendai&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Edo period")]

Although the Sendai area was inhabited as early as 20,000 years ago, the history of Sendai as a city begins from 1600, when the _[daimyō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daimy%C5%8D "Daimyō")_[Date Masamune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Date_Masamune "Date Masamune") relocated. Masamune was not happy with his previous stronghold, [Iwadeyama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iwadeyama,_Miyagi "Iwadeyama, Miyagi"), which was located in the northern portion of his territories and was difficult to access from [Edo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edo "Edo") (modern-day Tokyo). Sendai was an ideal location, being in the centre of Masamune's newly defined territories, upon the major road from Edo. [Tokugawa Ieyasu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokugawa_Ieyasu "Tokugawa Ieyasu") gave Masamune permission to build a new castle in Aobayama after the [Battle of Sekigahara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sekigahara "Battle of Sekigahara"). The previous ruler of the Sendai area had used a castle located on Aobayama. At this time Sendai was written as 千代 ("a thousand generations" or "eternity"). Masamune changed the _[kanji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanji "Kanji")_ to "仙臺", which later became "仙台" (literally: "hermit/wizard" plus "platform/plateau" or figuratively, "hermit on a platform/high ground"). The character came from a Chinese poem that praised a palace created by the [Emperor Wen of Han China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Wen_of_Han_China "Emperor Wen of Han China") (reigned 180–157 BCE), comparing it to a mythical palace in the [Kunlun Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunlun_Mountains "Kunlun Mountains"). Tradition says that Masamune chose this _kanji_ so that the castle would prosper as long as a mountain inhabited by an immortal hermit.

Masamune ordered the construction of [Sendai Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aoba_Castle "Aoba Castle") in December 1600 and the construction of the surrounding [castle town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_town "Castle town") in 1601. The grid plan roads in modern-day central Sendai are based upon his plans.

### Modern era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sendai&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Modern era")]

The first railway line between Sendai and Tokyo, now the [Tōhoku Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Dhoku_Main_Line "Tōhoku Main Line"), opened in 1887, bringing the area within a day's travel from Tokyo for the first time in history. [Tohoku Imperial University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tohoku_University "Tohoku University"), the region's first university, was founded in Sendai in 1907 and became the first Japanese university to admit female students in 1913.

Sendai was incorporated as a city on 1 April 1889, with the post-[Meiji restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiji_restoration "Meiji restoration") creation of the modern municipalities system following the [abolition of the han system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolition_of_the_han_system "Abolition of the han system"). At the time of incorporation, the city's area was 17.45 square kilometres (6.74 sq mi) and its population was 86,000. The city grew, however, through seven annexations that occurred between 1928 and 1988. The city became a [designated city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_designated_by_government_ordinance "City designated by government ordinance") on 1 April 1989; the city's population exceeded one million in 1999.

Sendai was considered to be one of Japan's greenest cities, mostly because of its great numbers of trees and plants. Sendai became known as The City of Trees before the [Meiji Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiji_Restoration "Meiji Restoration"), after the feudal [Sendai Domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai_Domain "Sendai Domain") encouraged residents to plant trees in their gardens. As a result, many houses, temples, and shrines in central Sendai had **household forests** (屋敷林, _yashikirin_), which were used as resources for wood and other everyday materials.

In 1925, the [Senseki Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senseki_Line "Senseki Line") to [Sendai Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai_Station_(Miyagi) "Sendai Station (Miyagi)") became the first underground railway segment in Japan, preceding the opening of the [Tokyo Metro Ginza Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Metro_Ginza_Line "Tokyo Metro Ginza Line") (Asia's first subway line) by two years.

The [2nd Infantry Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_Division_(Imperial_Japanese_Army) "2nd Division (Imperial Japanese Army)") was known as the "Sendai Division" as it was based in Sendai, and recruited locally. During the Second World War it was involved in many different campaigns, but one of the most important was the [Battle of Guadalcanal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Guadalcanal "Battle of Guadalcanal"). During the [bombing of Sendai during World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Sendai_during_World_War_II "Bombing of Sendai during World War II") by the United States on 10 July 1945, much of the historic center of the city was burned, with 2,755 inhabitants killed and 11,933 houses destroyed in the city.

### Postwar development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sendai&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Postwar development")]

Following World War II, the city was rebuilt, and Sendai became a vital transportation and logistics hub for the Tōhoku region with the construction of major arteries such as the [Tōhoku Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Dhoku_Expressway "Tōhoku Expressway") and [Tōhoku Shinkansen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Dhoku_Shinkansen "Tōhoku Shinkansen").

In the early 1950s, the [United States Army, Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army,_Japan "United States Army, Japan") operated Camp Schimmelpfennig and Camp Sendai in the city.

Sendai has been subject to several major earthquakes in recent history, including the [1978 Miyagi earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_Miyagi_earthquake "1978 Miyagi earthquake"), which was a catalyst for the development of Japan's current earthquake resistance standards, and the [2005 Miyagi earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Miyagi_earthquake "2005 Miyagi earthquake"). Most recently, the coastal area of Sendai, including [Sendai Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai_Airport "Sendai Airport"), was severely damaged in the [2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_T%C5%8Dhoku_earthquake_and_tsunami "2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai#cite_note-USGS-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai#cite_note-UKFO-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai#cite_note-TELG-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai#cite_note-7) The tsunami reportedly reached as far as [Wakabayashi Ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wakabayashi-ku,_Sendai "Wakabayashi-ku, Sendai") Office, 8 kilometers (5.0 mi) from the coastline. Thousands were killed, and countless more were injured and/or made homeless. Sendai's port was heavily damaged and temporarily closed, reopening on 16 April 2011.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai#cite_note-8)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sendai&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Geography")]

Sendai is located at lat. 38°16'05" north, long. 140°52'11" east. The city's area is 788.09 km 2 (304.28 sq mi), and stretches from the [Pacific Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") to the [Ōu Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%8Cu_Mountains "Ōu Mountains"), which are the east and west borders of Miyagi Prefecture. As a result, the city's geography is quite diverse. Eastern Sendai is a plains area, the center of the city is hilly, and western areas are mountainous. The highest point in the city is [Mount Funagata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Funagata "Mount Funagata") which stands 1,500 metres (4,921 feet)[above sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Above_mean_sea_level "Above mean sea level"). Unique among Japan's large coastal cities, Sendai's city core is built on a terrace at 40–60 m (131–197 ft) elevation.

The Sendai basin area is 939 km 2 (363 sq mi) (the mountainous area is 675 km 2 (261 sq mi), the plain area is 245 km 2 (95 sq mi) and the water body is 20 km 2 (8 sq mi)). The basin consists of urban areas, paddy fields and forests. The mid and upstream areas have forests. The [Natori River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natori_River "Natori River") flows through the area and reaches Sendai Bay after 55 km (34 mi).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai#cite_note-9)

The **Hirose River** (広瀬川, _Hirose-gawa_) flows 45 kilometres (28 miles) through Sendai. The river is well known as a symbol of Sendai, especially because it appears in the lyrics of Aoba-jō Koi-uta (青葉城恋唄; literally, _The Aoba Castle Love Song_), a popular song sung by Muneyuki Satō. [Aoba Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aoba_Castle "Aoba Castle") was built close to the river to use the river as a natural [moat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moat "Moat"). The river frequently flooded until the 1950s, but dams and levees constructed in the 1960s and 1970s have made such floods rare.

Most mountains in Sendai are dormant volcanoes, much older than the more famous [Mount Zaō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Za%C5%8D "Mount Zaō") and [Naruko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naruko_(volcano) "Naruko (volcano)") volcanoes in nearby municipalities. However, many [hot springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_springs "Hot springs") can be found in the city, indicating [hydrothermal activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrothermal_circulation "Hydrothermal circulation"). The Miyagi Oki [earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthquake "Earthquake") occurs offshore Sendai once every 25 to 40 years. The 7.2 magnitude [2005 Miyagi earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Miyagi_earthquake "2005 Miyagi earthquake"), which occurred on August 16, 2005, had an epicenter close to the _Miyagi Oki_ earthquake area. However, the Headquarters for Earthquake Research Promotion concluded that it was not the _Miyagi Oki_ earthquake, saying "...the recent event is not thought to be this earthquake. This is because the magnitude of the earthquake was small, and the source area, which was estimated from the aftershock distribution and seismic waves, didn't cover the whole expected source region. Although, the recent event ruptured a part of the focal region of the expected earthquake."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai#cite_note-10) In 2011, the 9.0 magnitude [2011 Tōhoku earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_T%C5%8Dhoku_earthquake_and_tsunami "2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami") occurred offshore Sendai, resulting in a devastating tsunami.

### Wards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sendai&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Wards")]

Sendai has five [wards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wards_of_Japan "Wards of Japan") ("ku"), which were created when it became a [designated city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities_designated_by_government_ordinance_of_Japan "Cities designated by government ordinance of Japan") in 1989. The city consciously avoided names that included directions (e.g., north [北](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E5%8C%97 "wikt:北"), center [中央](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E4%B8%AD%E5%A4%AE "wikt:中央")) when it chose names for the new wards.

## Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sendai&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Climate")]

Sendai has a [humid subtropical climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_subtropical_climate "Humid subtropical climate") ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification")_Cfa_), which features warm and wet summers, and cool and dry winters. Sendai summers are not as hot as [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo") to the south, while the winters are much milder than [Sapporo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapporo "Sapporo") to the north, but retains significant seasonal differences in temperature and rainfall. Extremes range from −11.7 to 37.4°C (10.9 to 99.3°F). Of Japan's prefectural capitals, Sendai experiences the fewest days of extreme temperatures (highs outside 0–30°C (32–86°F)) at 19.6 per year, compared to Tokyo's average of 49.

Winters are cool and relatively dry, with January temperatures averaging 1.5°C (34.7°F). Snowfall is much lower than cities on the [Sea of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_of_Japan "Sea of Japan") coast, such as [Niigata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niigata_(city) "Niigata (city)") and [Tottori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tottori_(city) "Tottori (city)"). Summers are very warm and much of the year's precipitation is delivered at this time, with an August average of 24.1°C (75.4°F). The city is rarely hit by [typhoons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhoon "Typhoon"), and experiences only 6 days with more than 10 centimetres (4 in) of rainfall on average. Sendai's [monsoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsoon "Monsoon") season usually begins in late April to early October, which is later than in most cities in Japan. During this season, cold winds from the Okhotsk air mass, called "[Yamase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamase "Yamase")", blow in and depress daytime highs.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai#cite_note-11)

The population density in this area was 6,879.9 persons per km 2, more than 5 times higher than the city's average population density at that time, 1,286.6 persons per km 2. Approximately 10,000 people in Sendai were non-Japanese citizens.

Sendai had 525,828 households in 2020. The average household had approximately 2.07 members. The average household was becoming smaller every year, because single-member households were increasing. At this time Sendai had more people in their early 50s and in their 20s and early 30s than in other age groups. This is a result of the first and second baby booms in Japan, and university students. The average age in Sendai is 38.4, which makes the city one of the youngest major cities in Japan.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai#cite_note-16)

## Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sendai&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Governance")]

[![Image 42](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Sendai_City_Hall_2023.jpg/250px-Sendai_City_Hall_2023.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sendai_City_Hall_2023.jpg)

Sendai City Hall

Sendai's political system is similar to other cities in Japan, because the [Local Autonomy Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Autonomy_Law "Local Autonomy Law") makes all municipalities uniform in terms of organization and power. However, Sendai is a designated city, so it has the same jurisdiction as [prefectures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefecture#Japanese_sense_of_prefecture "Prefecture") in some areas.

Sendai has a [mayor-council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor-council "Mayor-council") form of government with a directly elected mayor and a [unicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unicameral "Unicameral") city legislature. The [Sendai City Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_council "City council") members are elected from 5 elective districts, which correspond to the city's 5 wards. The number of assembly members allocated to each ward is based upon population. As of May 2005, the city has 60 assembly members; 17 from Aoba Ward, 11 from Miyagino, 8 from Wakabayashi, 13 from Taihaku, and 11 from Izumi. The City Assembly elects an Assembly Chairperson and Vice Chairperson. Sendai has two vice mayors, who are not elected by the populace. Miyagi contributes 24 seats to the Miyagi Prefectural legislature. In terms of national politics, the city is divided between the Miyagi 1st district and the Miyagi 2nd district of the [lower house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Representatives_of_Japan "House of Representatives of Japan") of the [Diet of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diet_of_Japan "Diet of Japan").
